summary_md: Session 4 opened with Scrum, the most used way of working in short cycles and, in the lecturer's words, the most commonly misapplied. This module teaches that first half from zero: the three accountabilities and who decides what in a self-managing team; the three artifacts and the commitment that stops each one being just a list; how to write a backlog item that is an outcome rather than a task; and the Definition of Done as the quality bar every Increment meets. It covers the five ceremonies, their time-boxes and what they are not, the pillars and values, and what Scrum does not give you: "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it." It ends with how the course maps Scrum onto the group project, where a green CI check is the Definition of Done and Checkpoint 1 is three binary items you can check yourself.
exam_focus_md:
- Short "who decides?" scenarios: a manager adding work mid-Sprint, a Scrum Master who assigns tasks, a Product Owner committee, a PO who prescribes how an item is built.
- Candidate backlog items or Definition of Done lines to judge: outcome or task, checkable or a wish, backlog or Definition of Done.
- A meeting described in a few lines (a Daily turned status report, a Review treated as applause, a Retrospective turned into blame) and which rule it breaks.
- Matching: artifact to commitment, ceremony to the question it answers or its time-box, Scrum term to its meaning in the course.
- Tool output as evidence about "done": a red CI step, a failing pytest line, a clean-clone check that breaks. The judgement is whether the item meets the Definition of Done, not how to silence the tool.
- Open answers in 5–8 lines: rewrite a weak backlog in words and justify the order; compare a task with an outcome as a backlog item; evaluate a team's Definition of Done; read a red CI step and decide whether `# type: ignore` makes an item done; explain why a team that runs every ceremony still ships nothing that works.

sections.heading: The problem Scrum answers
sections.body_md:
Session 2 showed why Waterfall fails for software, and session 4 opens by naming the problem Scrum answers: **"A year-long plan, written before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make."** Requirements change once the customer sees a first version, feedback arrives too late, and integration problems pile up until the end. Agile's answer is short cycles, working software and feedback: build a small slice, show it, learn, adjust.

Scrum is a framework for doing exactly that. In the slide's words it is "the most used way of doing that" and "also, the most commonly misapplied". Session 1 had already matched it to a problem: "No shared plan, four people build four corners" is answered by Agile and Scrum.

Scrum organises the work into **Sprints**: fixed-length cycles, each ending with something working that people can look at. The slides size every meeting for a two-week Sprint. Inside that cycle Scrum gives you three things, which the rest of this module takes in order:

| Scrum gives you | What they are |
|---|---|
| Accountabilities | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Artifacts | Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment, each with a commitment |
| Ceremonies | Refinement, Sprint Planning, Daily, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective |

Why "most misapplied"? The visible parts (a fifteen-minute standing meeting, a board, someone called Scrum Master) are easy to copy. The parts that make it work are not: a working Increment every Sprint, honest feedback that changes the plan, and a team that decides how to do its own work. A company can rename its weekly status meeting "Daily Scrum", keep its eighteen-month plan, and believe it does Scrum. Slide 14 calls this "mocking the Scrum ceremonies", and section 8 comes back to it: "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it."

Session 2 also placed Scrum among other Agile methods (Kanban, XP, Lean) and said the course borrows from more than one: Scrum vocabulary for the project, XP's engineering practices (TDD, CI, small commits) as the technical spine, and a Kanban board to track the group's work. "It is not about picking one methodology and following blindly."
key_points: Scrum answers "a year-long plan, written before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make".
A Sprint is a fixed-length cycle that ends with something working; the slides size every meeting for two weeks.
The most used Agile framework, and the most commonly misapplied: the ceremonies are easy to copy, working software is not.
sections.exam_note_md: Expect a scenario where the vocabulary is present and the substance missing. The judgement is that renamed meetings on top of a fixed long plan are not Scrum.

sections.heading: Three accountabilities
sections.body_md:
A Scrum team has three accountabilities. The slide's table, titled "The Agile team", gives each one a line:

| Role | Accountable for |
|---|---|
| **Product Owner** (PO) | The value of the product. Owns and orders the Product Backlog. One person, not a committee |
| **Scrum Master** | Ensures the process works. Removes impediments; coaches. Not a manager |
| **Developers** | Building the Increment. Cross-functional, self-managing |

**Product Owner.** The PO decides what is worth building and in what order, because the PO answers for the value the product delivers. It is one person so that there is one order and one place where every request ends up. A committee that votes on the order each week produces compromises and leaves nobody accountable when the order is wrong.

**Scrum Master.** The Scrum Master looks after the process, not other people's tasks. An **impediment** is anything blocking the Developers: an access right that never arrives, a stakeholder who keeps interrupting, a problem nobody inside the team can fix. The Scrum Master removes it, and coaches the team on how Scrum works. "Not a manager" means the Scrum Master does not hand out work, does not collect status reports and does not decide whether an item is done.

**Developers.** Everyone who builds the **Increment**, the working product a Sprint adds to. **Cross-functional** means that between them they have every skill needed to finish an item (code, tests, documentation) without waiting for another department. **Self-managing** is the subject of the next section.

Two more lines on the slide set the shape of the team:

- The team should ideally consist of **ten people or fewer**. The Daily alone shows why: at about a minute per developer, a team of twenty could not fit it into fifteen minutes.
- **Hierarchy stays as horizontal as possible.** There is no lead who assigns tickets. The PO decides what, the Developers decide how, the Scrum Master protects the process.

In the course the mapping is simple: the Product Owner is the lecturer and the Developers are your group (section 9).
key_points: Product Owner: the value of the product; owns and orders the Product Backlog; one person, not a committee.
Scrum Master: ensures the process works, removes impediments, coaches. Not a manager.
Developers: build the Increment; cross-functional and self-managing.
Ten people or fewer; hierarchy as horizontal as possible.

sections.heading: Self-managing: who decides what
sections.body_md:
Slide 7 spells out what "self-managing" means in three lines:

1. **The team decides how the work is done, and who does what.**
2. **The Product Owner decides what is worth doing, and in what order.**
3. **Nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint.**

Each line removes a familiar habit. The first removes the manager who assigns tickets to named people and prescribes the technique. If Ana is better at pricing rules and Pol at the command-line interface, the Developers arrange that themselves, and they choose how to build it.

The second keeps the decision about value in one place. The PO does not tell the team how to build an item, but the PO alone puts the items in order. "Weighted averages is next" is the PO's call. "Joan should do it with a dictionary" is not: that is who and how, which belong to the Developers. Careful reading matters here, because both can be said in one sentence.

The third protects the Sprint. At Sprint Planning the team agrees what will be delivered by the end of the Sprint. If a director outside the team can push extra work in halfway through, the Sprint Goal stops meaning anything and the team's own plan stops counting. A new request does not vanish: it goes to the Product Owner, who places it in the Product Backlog, where it competes on value with everything else and can be picked at the next Sprint Planning.

A worked example. Halfway through a two-week Sprint, the head of sales stops by:

> "Add CSV export and a monthly chart to this Sprint, and have Marc do the chart tonight."

Three rules are broken. Someone outside the team is deciding how much goes into the Sprint; someone outside is deciding who does what; and the request skipped the PO, who decides what is worth doing and in what order. The Scrum Master's job is to make the process work: send the request to the PO and keep the Sprint intact. Only the PO can cancel a Sprint, and that almost never happens.

Self-managing is not "no rules". The team still works to a Sprint Goal it agreed, inside time-boxes, to a Definition of Done. It is the freedom to decide how to meet them.
key_points: How the work is done and who does what: the Developers.
What is worth doing and in what order: the Product Owner.
Nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint; outside requests go to the PO and the Product Backlog.

sections.heading: Three artifacts, three commitments
sections.body_md:
Scrum has three artifacts. Each exists to make something visible, and each has a **commitment**: the thing it is measured against.

| Artifact | What it makes visible | Commitment |
|---|---|---|
| **Product Backlog** | Everything the product might need, in order | **Product Goal** |
| **Sprint Backlog** | What this Sprint will deliver, and the plan for it | **Sprint Goal** |
| **Increment** | The working product built so far | **Definition of Done** |

The slide's line to remember: **"Without its commitment, it is just a list."**

- A Product Backlog without a Product Goal (the longer-term objective the product works towards) is a wish list with no reason to say no to anything.
- A Sprint Backlog without a Sprint Goal is a pile of tickets. The Daily asks "Are we on track for the Sprint Goal?"; with no goal nobody can answer, and every item looks equally urgent.
- An Increment without a Definition of Done is "it works on my laptop". Nobody can say whether it is finished, so nobody can say whether it ships.

**The Product Backlog** gets its own slide: **"Ordered. Emergent. Never finished."**

- **Ordered by the Product Owner, top = next.** Position is a decision, not an accident.
- **Emergent, never finished.** New items appear as people use the product and learn; old ones change or disappear. A backlog that is "complete" is a requirements document in disguise.
- **Items are outcomes, not tasks.** The slide's example: "a returning user can log in with an email link". Section 5 shows how to write them.
- **Refined continuously, in detail only near the top.** The items you will build next get the detail; the rest stay rough.

Why only near the top? Because the bottom will change before anyone builds it: **"Estimating item 40 precisely is waste: it will change before it is built."** The backlog brief applies this to your group: only the top three items need detail, because "the rest will change, and detailing them now is wasted work". It is session 2's lesson again: a plan written in full detail before anything is built is the Waterfall assumption that software keeps breaking.
key_points: Product Backlog → Product Goal; Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal; Increment → Definition of Done.
"Without its commitment, it is just a list."
The Product Backlog is ordered, emergent and never finished; ordered by the PO, top = next.
Detail only near the top: "estimating item 40 precisely is waste".
sections.exam_note_md: Matching artifact to commitment is a core question; the exam version shows a team without a Sprint Goal or with a fully estimated backlog and asks what is wrong.

sections.heading: Writing a usable backlog item
sections.body_md:
The backlog brief (the session 4 workshop) defines an item: **"an outcome a user gets, not a task you perform. It is small enough to finish in a sitting, and you can tell when it is done."** It gives the shape:

> `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>.`

The **"so that"** is, in the brief's words, "the part that stops you building something nobody needs". It names the benefit, so the Product Owner can weigh the item against others, and so the team notices when an item has no benefit at all.

The brief's three worked examples come from the expense tracker, and each became real code:

| Item | What it became |
|---|---|
| As a user, I can see a total per category, so that I know where the money went | The first thing it ever did |
| As a user, I can report on one category only, so that I can look at dining without the noise | `--category` |
| As a user, I can add an expense from the command line, so that I do not edit a CSV by hand | `expenses add` |

And three that are **not** usable as items:

- **"Do the CSV part"**: a task, not an outcome. Nobody can tell when it is done.
- **"Make the code good"**: not checkable. Quality belongs in the Definition of Done.
- **"Write tests"**: every item is tested, so it is a standard, not a backlog entry. It belongs in the Definition of Done too.

Slide 30 gives rewrites. Instead of "Do the CSV part", write "A user can add an expense and see it in the next report". Instead of "Make it good", write "Invalid input prints a message and exits non-zero". Both can be checked by running the program.

Finally, **ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start**. For the parking-lot topic, coloured output is easy and pleasant to build first, but nobody gets anything until a ticket can be issued and a stay priced. A sensible top three:

1. As an attendant, I can issue a ticket for a plate number, so that I know which car is in which space.
2. As a driver, I can see the price of my stay when I leave, so that I pay the right amount.
3. As an attendant, I can see how many spaces are free, so that I can turn cars away before the barrier.

Those three get detail. The other five or more stay one line each until they move up.
key_points: `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>.` The "so that" stops you building something nobody needs.
An item is an outcome a user gets, small enough to finish in a sitting, and you can tell when it is done.
Tasks ("Do the CSV part") are not items; standards ("Make the code good", "Write tests") go in the Definition of Done.
Ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start.

sections.heading: The Definition of Done
sections.body_md:
The **Definition of Done** (DoD) is, in slide 10's words, "the quality bar every Increment meets", "decided once, applied to everything". It is not a checklist written fresh for each item: it is one list, the same for every item, every Sprint.

The slide names the classic contents: **compiles · tested · reviewed · documented · deployable**. Two rules follow:

- **"Done except for tests" is not admissible.** There is no partly done. The item meets the bar or it does not.
- **"An item that misses the Definition of Done is not done, and does not ship."** It is not presented as finished at the Review and it does not go into the Increment.

The backlog brief says how to write one: **"Write it as things you can check, not things you can hope."** Compare:

| A hope | Something you can check |
|---|---|
| The code is clean | The CI check is green |
| We test thoroughly | There is at least one test for the new behaviour |
| It is easy to use | The README says how to use the new behaviour |
| It handles errors well | Bad input prints a message and exits non-zero |
| We work as a team | Another member of the group has read the change |

Every line on the right can be answered yes or no by someone who was not in the room; they come from the brief's starter list, which also has "The code runs from a clean clone: `uv sync && uv run <your-app> --help`". The brief says to edit that list, not copy it.

Two lines from the course are worth knowing by heart:

- **"A Definition of Done with six items you ignore is worse than three you keep."** An ignored line is worse than no line: the list then claims a standard the work does not meet, and everyone learns that the DoD is decoration. "Cut what you will not honour."
- **"A Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish."**

Why "Write tests" belongs here and not in the backlog: tests are not something a user gets; they are part of what "done" means for every item. "Make the code good" is the same kind of thing. The backlog holds outcomes; the DoD holds the standard each outcome is built to.

When he set the backlog task (slide 29), the lecturer added: "I hold you to your own Definition of Done in November." The one line that is not yours to choose is the green CI check (section 9).
key_points: The quality bar every Increment meets, decided once and applied to everything.
Compiles · tested · reviewed · documented · deployable. "Done except for tests" is not done.
An item that misses the DoD is not done and does not ship.
Write lines you can check, not hope. Six ignored lines are worse than three you keep.
sections.exam_note_md: Tool output can be the evidence: a red CI step or a failing test means the item is not done, whatever its author says. Candidate DoD lines are judged as checkable or a wish.

sections.heading: The ceremonies, and what they are not
sections.body_md:
Scrum's ceremonies are meetings scheduled within each Sprint. Each is **time-boxed**: it has a maximum length, sized to the Sprint. Slide 11 gives the time-boxes for a two-week Sprint and the question each ceremony answers:

| Ceremony | Time-box (2-week Sprint) | Question |
|---|---|---|
| Refinement | ~4h | The PO and Developers discuss implementation details for increments |
| Sprint Planning | 1h | Agree on what will be delivered at the end of the Sprint |
| Daily | 15 min | Are we on track for the Sprint Goal? |
| Sprint Review | 1h | What was built; what should change |
| Sprint Retrospective | 1h | How the team worked, and what to improve |

The time-boxes scale: **shorter Sprint, proportionally shorter events; longer Sprint, proportionally longer events**. A one-week Sprint gets a Review of about thirty minutes. Books and websites on Scrum give other maximums and treat Refinement as an activity rather than a meeting; for this course, and this exam, use the slide's table.

Separate the two meetings at the end carefully. The **Review** looks at the product: what was built, and what should change in the backlog. The **Retrospective** looks at the team: how it worked, and what it will do differently.

Slide 12 says what the ceremonies are **not**:

- **The Daily Scrum is not a status report to a manager.** It is fifteen minutes, for the Developers. The PO can join but is not expected to participate. Each developer takes about a minute to state their latest work, what they intend to work on next, and whether they have any blockers. A long technical discussion does not fit in that minute; a blocker that needs outside help is an impediment for the Scrum Master.
- **The Review is not a demo for applause.** Stakeholders come to give feedback and change the backlog. A Review where everybody claps and the backlog stays the same has inspected nothing.
- **The Retrospective is not blame.** It is a team discussion of what worked, what did not, and what changes can be introduced accordingly. "Whose push broke CI?" is the wrong question; "what change stops a broken push reaching `main`?" is the right one.
- **The PO retains the power to cancel the Sprint**, for instance when its goal no longer makes sense. This almost never happens.

Refinement is where the top of the backlog gets its detail (section 4). Sprint Planning is where the team, not someone outside, agrees what the Sprint will deliver (section 3).
key_points: Two-week Sprint: Refinement ~4h, Sprint Planning 1h, Daily 15 min, Review 1h, Retrospective 1h; scale with Sprint length.
Daily: for the Developers; latest work, next work, blockers, about a minute each. Not a status report to a manager.
Review looks at the product and changes the backlog; Retrospective looks at how the team worked. Not applause, not blame.
The Product Owner retains the power to cancel a Sprint; it almost never happens.
sections.exam_note_md: A meeting is described in a few lines and you say which rule it breaks. Read Review versus Retrospective carefully: one looks at the product, the other at the team.

sections.heading: Pillars, values, and what Scrum does not give you
sections.body_md:
Scrum rests on three **pillars**: **transparency · inspection · adaptation**. Make the real state of the work visible, look at it regularly, and change course when what you see calls for it. Each ceremony is an inspection point: the Daily inspects progress towards the Sprint Goal, the Review inspects the Increment, the Retrospective inspects how the team works.

It names five **values**: **commitment · focus · openness · respect · courage**.

Slide 13 links them in two lines worth quoting exactly:

- **"Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction."** If the board says an item is done while its tests fail, the Review inspects the board, not the product. Everyone is pleased, and nothing true was learned.
- **"Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times."** If the Retrospective names the same problem every Sprint and nobody is willing to change anything (tell a teammate, tell the PO the goal was too big), the team repeats the same Sprint until the project ends.

**What Scrum does not give you.** Slide 14 is blunt:

- No requirements document.
- No promise about what is in version 1.0, a year out.
- No architecture, no testing strategy, no engineering practices at all.

**"Scrum organises the work; it does not do it."** The slide warns of two opposite mistakes: imitating Agile by mocking the Scrum ceremonies, and the "equally dangerous tendency" to believe that following the ceremonies is enough to get real work done. A team can hold every Daily on time, run a cheerful Review and a polite Retrospective, and still ship nothing that installs, passes its tests or runs on another machine. Ceremonies performed for their own sake, with nothing working at the end, are sometimes called **cargo-cult** Scrum: the form without the substance.

This is why the course pairs Scrum with XP's engineering practices (TDD, CI, small commits) and why its Definition of Done is a check a machine runs. Scrum supplies the rhythm, the roles and the ordered backlog; the tests, the type checker and the CI check do the part Scrum leaves out.
key_points: Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation. Values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage.
"Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction."
"Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times."
"Scrum organises the work; it does not do it": no requirements document, no v1.0 promise, no engineering practices.
sections.exam_note_md: A likely open question: a team runs every ceremony and ships nothing that works. Answer with slide 14, then name what is missing (the DoD, engineering practices).

sections.heading: Scrum in this course
sections.body_md:
The course runs the group project with Scrum's vocabulary. Slide 16's mapping:

| Scrum | This course |
|---|---|
| Sprint | The stretch between two checkpoints |
| Sprint Goal | The checkpoint's deliverable |
| Definition of Done | A green CI check, the same one for all groups |
| Product Owner | The lecturer |
| Developers | Your group of four |
| Sprint Review | Practice sessions, and Demo Day |

In practice the lecturer, as Product Owner, sets each Sprint Goal (the checkpoint's deliverable); inside that goal, the backlog brief asks your group to write and order its own backlog by value.

So the stretch ending at CP1 (Friday 25 September) was a Sprint, and its Sprint Goal was CP1's deliverable: the template turned into your project, with one real command, tagged `v0.1`.

**The green CI check is the line of the DoD that is not yours to choose.** The project brief calls it "the referee, not the judge": the automated `ruff` + `mypy` + `pytest` run on every push "is not marked itself, but a red check means the submission is not mechanically valid". The backlog brief adds that it is the same check for every group and "runs on a machine none of us owns", so "it works on my laptop" does not count. The partial-submission rubric makes it concrete: if CI is red on the `v0.5` commit, the Tests criterion is capped at 1.

**CP1 as a Definition of Done.** Slide 17 calls it "public, binary and checkable before you submit":

1. `uv sync && uv run <your-app> --help` works from a clean clone
2. `src/` layout, package importable
3. README says what the program does and how to run it (session 5's slide 14: what it does, how to install, how to run)

and adds: **"A Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish."** The scaffold lab shows how to check item 1 the way the marker does: clone into an empty folder and run the commands there. A clean clone "has no `.venv`, no caches and nothing you forgot to commit", so it catches the file that only exists on your laptop. On the expense tracker at `v0.1`, in a fresh clone, the check passes (uv's build lines and package list trimmed):

```console
$ uv sync && uv run expenses --help
Using CPython 3.13.15
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 9 packages in 4ms
Installed 8 packages in 6ms

 Usage: expenses [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 A terminal expense tracker.

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --install-completion          Install completion for the current shell.      │
│ --show-completion             Show completion for the current shell, to copy │
│                               it or customize the installation.              │
│ --help                        Show this message and exit.                    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Commands ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ report                                                                       │
│ add                                                                          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

Your own Definition of Done adds lines on top of the green check, such as a test for the new behaviour, a README line, a teammate who has read the change. The lecturer holds each group to its own.
key_points: Sprint = the stretch between two checkpoints; Sprint Goal = the checkpoint's deliverable.
Definition of Done = a green CI check, the same for all groups: the referee, not the judge.
Product Owner = the lecturer; Developers = your group; Sprint Review = practice sessions and Demo Day.
CP1: three binary items you can check yourself, from a clean clone.

traps: **"The Scrum Master is the team's manager."** No: the Scrum Master ensures the process works, removes impediments and coaches. The Developers decide who does what; nobody hands out tasks.
**"A committee can be the Product Owner."** The slide says one person, not a committee: one person owns and orders the Product Backlog, so there is one order and one place for requests to go.
**"A senior manager can add urgent work to the running Sprint."** Nobody outside the team decides how much goes into a Sprint. The request goes to the Product Owner and into the Product Backlog.

**"A good backlog is fully detailed and estimated up front."** Only the top needs detail (the top three, in the brief); estimating item 40 precisely is waste because it will change before it is built.
**"Write tests" and "Make the code good" are backlog items.** They are standards every item meets, so they belong in the Definition of Done. Backlog items are outcomes a user gets.
**"Done except for tests" is nearly done.** It is not admissible: an item that misses the Definition of Done is not done and does not ship.
**A longer Definition of Done is a stricter one.** Six lines you ignore are worse than three you keep, and a line you cannot check yourself is a wish.

**The Daily is where developers report status to the manager or the PO.** It is fifteen minutes for the Developers, about the Sprint Goal: latest work, next work, blockers. The PO can join but is not expected to participate.
**The Sprint Review is a demo to show off the work.** Stakeholders come to give feedback and change the backlog; applause with an unchanged backlog means nothing was inspected.

**Holding all the ceremonies means you are doing Scrum, and working software will follow.** Scrum organises the work; it does not do it. It gives no requirements document, no testing strategy and no engineering practices.

flashcards.front_md: What problem does Scrum answer, according to session 4?
flashcards.back_md: "A year-long plan, written before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make." Agile replaces it with short cycles, working software and feedback; Scrum is the most used way of doing that.

flashcards.front_md: Why does the slide call Scrum "the most commonly misapplied"?
flashcards.back_md: Its visible parts (meetings, a board, a Scrum Master) are easy to copy without the substance: a working Increment every Sprint, feedback that changes the plan, a team that decides how to work.

flashcards.front_md: What is the Product Owner accountable for?
flashcards.back_md: The value of the product. Owns and orders the Product Backlog. One person, not a committee.

flashcards.front_md: What is the Scrum Master accountable for?
flashcards.back_md: Ensures the process works. Removes impediments; coaches. Not a manager.

flashcards.front_md: What are the Developers accountable for, and how big should the team be?
flashcards.back_md: Building the Increment; cross-functional and self-managing. Ideally ten people or fewer, with hierarchy as horizontal as possible.

flashcards.front_md: Self-managing: who decides how, who decides what, who decides how much?
flashcards.back_md: The team decides how the work is done and who does what. The PO decides what is worth doing and in what order. Nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint.

flashcards.front_md: Mid-Sprint, the head of sales wants a feature added now. Where does the request go?
flashcards.back_md: To the Product Owner, who orders it in the Product Backlog; it can be picked at the next Sprint Planning. Only the PO could cancel the Sprint, which almost never happens.

flashcards.front_md: Match each artifact to its commitment.
flashcards.back_md: Product Backlog → Product Goal. Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal. Increment → Definition of Done.

flashcards.front_md: "Without its commitment, it is just a list." Give an example.
flashcards.back_md: A Sprint Backlog with no Sprint Goal: the Daily cannot answer "are we on track for the Sprint Goal?", and every item looks equally urgent.

flashcards.front_md: The three words on the Product Backlog slide?
flashcards.back_md: Ordered. Emergent. Never finished. Ordered by the PO, top = next; refined continuously, in detail only near the top.

flashcards.front_md:
CI on the item's commit ends like this, and its author says "done apart from one test". What does it mean for the item?

```text
E       assert 15.0 == 10.0
E        +  where 15.0 = overdue_fine(30)

FAILED tests/test_fines.py::test_fine_is_capped - assert 15.0 == 10.0
```
flashcards.back_md: The fine is not capped: `overdue_fine(30)` returns 15.0 where the test expects 10.0. CI is red, so the item misses the Definition of Done: it is not done, does not ship, and is not shown as finished at the Review.

flashcards.front_md: The shape of a backlog item in the brief?
flashcards.back_md: `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>.` An outcome a user gets, small enough to finish in a sitting, and you can tell when it is done.

flashcards.front_md: What does the "so that" part of an item do?
flashcards.back_md: It names the benefit: "the part that stops you building something nobody needs". It also gives the PO something to order by.

flashcards.front_md: Why is "Do the CSV part" not a usable item?
flashcards.back_md: A task, not an outcome: nobody can tell when it is done. Rewrite: "A user can add an expense and see it in the next report".

flashcards.front_md: Why are "Make the code good" and "Write tests" not backlog items?
flashcards.back_md: They are standards every item meets, so they belong in the Definition of Done. "Make the code good" is also not checkable.

flashcards.front_md: How is the Product Backlog ordered?
flashcards.back_md: By value, not by what is easiest to start. The top is what you build next.

flashcards.front_md: What is the Definition of Done, and its classic contents?
flashcards.back_md: The quality bar every Increment meets, decided once, applied to everything. Compiles · tested · reviewed · documented · deployable.

flashcards.front_md: An item meets everything except its tests. Is it done?
flashcards.back_md: No. "Done except for tests" is not admissible. An item that misses the DoD is not done and does not ship.

flashcards.front_md: A DoD line you can check versus a wish: one example of each.
flashcards.back_md: Check: "The CI check is green", "Bad input prints a message and exits non-zero". Wish: "The code is clean". A DoD you cannot check yourself is a wish.

flashcards.front_md: Why is a DoD with six ignored items worse than three you keep?
flashcards.back_md: Ignored lines claim a standard the work does not meet and teach everyone the DoD is decoration. "Cut what you will not honour."

flashcards.front_md: Time-boxes for a two-week Sprint?
flashcards.back_md: Refinement ~4h · Sprint Planning 1h · Daily 15 min · Sprint Review 1h · Sprint Retrospective 1h. Shorter Sprint, proportionally shorter events; longer, longer.

flashcards.front_md: What does each developer say at the Daily, and to whom?
flashcards.back_md: About a minute each, to the other Developers: latest work, what they intend to work on next, any blockers. Not a status report to a manager.

flashcards.front_md: Sprint Review versus Sprint Retrospective?
flashcards.back_md: Review: the product. What was built and what should change; stakeholders give feedback and change the backlog. Retrospective: the team. How it worked and what to improve; not blame.

flashcards.front_md: Who can cancel a Sprint?
flashcards.back_md: The Product Owner. It almost never happens.

flashcards.front_md: Scrum's three pillars and five values?
flashcards.back_md: Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation. Values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage.

flashcards.front_md: "Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction." What does it mean in practice?
flashcards.back_md: If the real state is hidden (items shown as done while CI is red), the Review inspects a story, not the product, and nothing true is learned.

flashcards.front_md: "Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times." What does it mean in practice?
flashcards.back_md: The Retrospective names the same problem every Sprint, but nobody dares change anything, so the team repeats the same Sprint.

flashcards.front_md: What does Scrum not give you?
flashcards.back_md: No requirements document; no promise about v1.0 a year out; no architecture, testing strategy or engineering practices. "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it."

flashcards.front_md: The course mapping: Sprint, Sprint Goal, DoD, PO, Developers, Sprint Review?
flashcards.back_md: The stretch between two checkpoints; the checkpoint's deliverable; a green CI check, the same for all groups; the lecturer; your group; practice sessions and Demo Day.

flashcards.front_md: CP1's three binary items, and why check them from a clean clone?
flashcards.back_md: `uv sync && uv run <your-app> --help` works from a clean clone; `src/` layout, package importable; README says what it does and how to run it. A clean clone has nothing you forgot to commit.

questions.stem_md: Session 1 matched each way working code fails to the method or tool that answers it, and session 4 opened with "the problem Scrum answers". Which problem is Scrum the answer to?

options.text_md: Code that runs on one developer's laptop and on no other machine
options.why_md: That is "works on my machine", answered by a standard setup, the lockfile and containers, not by a way of organising work.

options.text_md: A long plan made up front, on estimates nobody can make
options.why_md: The slide's own problem: "a year-long plan, written before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make". Scrum replaces it with short Sprints that each end in working software and feedback.

options.text_md: Code that nobody can read six months after it was written
options.why_md: Unreadable code is answered by clean code, testing and TDD (module 2). Scrum says nothing about how code is written.

options.text_md: A teammate's change that silently breaks the build
options.why_md: That is answered by version control, code review and CI. Scrum gives no engineering practices.

questions.explanation_md: Session 4's first Scrum slide states the problem: "A year-long plan, written before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make." Agile moves to short cycles, working software and feedback, and Scrum is the most used way of doing that. Session 1's mapping agrees: "No shared plan → Agile, Scrum". The other three are real problems, but each has its own answer in the course: a standard setup and containers for "works on my machine", clean code and tests for code nobody can read, version control and CI for broken builds. Scrum organises the work; it does not fix the code.

questions.stem_md: A logistics company announces it "has gone Scrum". The weekly status meeting is renamed the Daily Scrum; it still takes an hour, with each person reporting to the department head, who now has the title Scrum Master. The eighteen-month plan signed off in January is unchanged, and nothing is shown to users until it is complete. Which description fits best?

options.text_md: It is Scrum: it now has a Daily, a Scrum Master and a plan the team follows
options.why_md: Having the names is not doing Scrum. This is the "most commonly misapplied" case: roles and meetings without short cycles of working software.

options.text_md: It is Kanban, because the work is not split into Sprints and nothing is time-boxed
options.why_md: Kanban is a board with a limit on work in progress, pulling items when there is capacity; none of that is here. The label misses the real problem.

options.text_md: It is a fair use of Scrum for a large company, where a longer Daily is normal
options.why_md: Time-boxes scale with Sprint length, not with company size, and the Daily is never a status report to a manager.

options.text_md: Scrum's names on top of a Waterfall plan: no short cycles, no feedback
options.why_md: It copies the ceremonies and keeps the long plan written before anything is built, which is exactly the problem Scrum answers. Renaming the meetings leaves it untouched: no short cycles, no working software, no feedback.

questions.explanation_md: Session 4 calls Scrum the most used way of working in short cycles, and the most commonly misapplied. This company shows how: the vocabulary changed, the plan did not. An eighteen-month plan signed off up front, with no user feedback until the end, is Waterfall. The "Daily" breaks two rules from slide 12 (it is a status report to a manager, and it runs four times its fifteen minutes), and the "Scrum Master" is a manager, which slide 6 says the role is not. Slide 14 names the mistake: imitating Agile by mocking the Scrum ceremonies.

questions.stem_md: Sort each statement into the accountability it describes.

items.text_md: Accountable for the value of the product
items.why_md: Value is the PO's accountability: deciding what is worth building.

items.text_md: Owns and orders the Product Backlog; top = next
items.why_md: One person owns and orders the backlog, so there is one order.

items.text_md: Can cancel the Sprint, though this almost never happens
items.why_md: Slide 12: the PO retains the power to cancel the Sprint, though this almost never happens.

items.text_md: Ensures the process works
items.why_md: The first words of the Scrum Master's row on slide 6.

items.text_md: Removes impediments, such as a missing access right or a stakeholder who keeps interrupting
items.why_md: Removing what blocks the Developers is the Scrum Master's job, without managing them.

items.text_md: Coaches the team on how Scrum works, without being its manager
items.why_md: Coaching, not managing: the slide says "Not a manager".

items.text_md: Builds the Increment
items.why_md: The Developers are accountable for building the Increment.

items.text_md: Has, between its members, every skill needed to get an item done
items.why_md: That is what cross-functional means.

items.text_md: Decides how the work is done and who does what
items.why_md: Self-managing: how and who belong to the team (slide 7).

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6 gives each accountability one line: the PO is accountable for the value of the product and owns and orders the Product Backlog; the Scrum Master ensures the process works, removes impediments and coaches, and is not a manager; the Developers build the Increment and are cross-functional and self-managing. Two items test details from elsewhere in session 4: deciding how and who belongs to the self-managing team (slide 7), and the power to cancel a Sprint belongs to the PO (slide 12).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the Scrum Master matches session 4?

options.text_md: Assigns the Sprint's tasks to Developers and checks they are finished
options.why_md: That is a manager's job, and the slide says the Scrum Master is not a manager. The Developers decide who does what.

options.text_md: Owns the Product Backlog and decides which item comes next
options.why_md: Owning and ordering the backlog is the Product Owner's accountability.

options.text_md: Ensures the process works, removes impediments and coaches the team
options.why_md: The slide's own row: "Ensures the process works. Removes impediments; coaches. Not a manager."

options.text_md: Collects a status report from each developer at the Daily
options.why_md: The Daily is fifteen minutes for the Developers, not a status report to anyone.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6's row for the Scrum Master: "Ensures the process works. Removes impediments; coaches. Not a manager." Each wrong option turns the role into something it is not: a manager who assigns tasks (slide 7 gives "who does what" to the team), the Product Owner (who owns and orders the backlog), or a manager receiving status reports (slide 12: the Daily "is not a status report to a manager"). An impediment is anything blocking the Developers, and removing it serves the team rather than directing it.

questions.stem_md: A bank sets up a Scrum team for a new savings app. Instead of one Product Owner, a steering group of five department heads meets every Monday and votes on the order of the Product Backlog; ties are carried over to the next week. According to session 4, what is the problem?

options.text_md: None: a weekly vote among five heads is fairer than one person's opinion
options.why_md: Fairness is not the point. With a committee nobody is accountable for the value of the product, and the order shifts with every vote.

options.text_md: The Product Owner must be one person, who owns and orders the backlog
options.why_md: The slide: "One person, not a committee", accountable for the value of the product. One person gives one order and someone accountable for it.

options.text_md: The Scrum Master should own the order, so it stays neutral between departments
options.why_md: The Scrum Master ensures the process works; ordering the backlog is the Product Owner's accountability.

options.text_md: The Developers should join the vote, so the order reflects what is easiest to build
options.why_md: Developers decide how, not what, and the backlog is ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6 says the Product Owner is "one person, not a committee". One person owns and orders the backlog, so there is one order, one place where requests go, and someone accountable when the order turns out to be wrong. A weekly vote with carried-over ties means the team often has no clear top item, which is exactly what "top = next" is meant to give it. The wrong options move the decision to roles that do not own it, or reorder by ease instead of value.

questions.stem_md: Day 6 of a two-week Sprint. The marketing director, who is not on the team, emails two developers: "Please add PDF export to this Sprint, it's for a client meeting on Friday." The Sprint Goal does not include export. What does session 4 say should happen?

options.text_md: It goes to the Product Owner, who decides where it sits in the Product Backlog
options.why_md: Slide 7: nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint, and the PO decides what is worth doing and in what order.

options.text_md: The developers add it to the Sprint, because the request comes from someone senior
options.why_md: Seniority outside the team does not change the rule: nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint.

options.text_md: The Scrum Master decides whether the Sprint has room for it
options.why_md: The Scrum Master makes the process work; here the process says the request goes to the PO.

options.text_md: The developers work evenings to fit it in without touching the Sprint Goal
options.why_md: Extra hours hide the problem and the request still bypasses the PO. Session 2's principles also ask for a pace sustainable indefinitely.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7: "Nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint", and "The Product Owner decides what is worth doing, and in what order." The director's request is legitimate input, but it goes to the PO, who places it in the Product Backlog where it competes on value with everything else and can be picked at the next Sprint Planning. If it really cannot wait, that is the PO's decision to take, up to cancelling the Sprint, which almost never happens.

questions.stem_md: At Refinement, the Product Owner of a school-software team says: "Weighted averages is the next item. Joan should do it, and she should store the weights in a dictionary." Which part of this oversteps the Product Owner's role?

options.text_md: Saying which item is next, since the Developers decide the order
options.why_md: Ordering is exactly the PO's job: "what is worth doing, and in what order".

options.text_md: Only prescribing the dictionary; naming Joan is fine, since the PO knows who is free
options.why_md: Who does what is also the team's decision (slide 7). Knowing who is free does not make it the PO's call.

options.text_md: Only naming Joan; prescribing the dictionary is fine, since the PO owns the item
options.why_md: Owning the item means deciding what it must achieve and where it sits in the order, not how it is built.

options.text_md: Naming Joan and prescribing a dictionary: who and how belong to the Developers
options.why_md: Slide 7: the team decides how the work is done and who does what. Saying which item is next stays the PO's call.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7 splits the decisions. "The Product Owner decides what is worth doing, and in what order": saying weighted averages comes next is the PO's call. "The team decides how the work is done, and who does what": who takes the item and which data structure to use are the Developers' decisions. The PO can say what the item must achieve (a correct average with weights per assignment); the Developers decide how to deliver it. The two halves of one sentence get different answers, which is why this needs careful reading.

questions.stem_md: Each Scrum artifact has a commitment. Which pairing is correct?

options.text_md: Increment → Definition of Done
options.why_md: The DoD is the quality bar every Increment meets.

options.text_md: Product Backlog → Sprint Goal
options.why_md: The Product Backlog commits to the Product Goal; the Sprint Goal belongs to the Sprint Backlog.

options.text_md: Sprint Backlog → Definition of Done
options.why_md: The Sprint Backlog commits to the Sprint Goal; the DoD is the Increment's bar.

options.text_md: Increment → Product Goal
options.why_md: The Product Goal is what the whole Product Backlog works towards, not the quality bar of one Increment.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 8: Product Backlog → Product Goal; Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal; Increment → Definition of Done. One way to remember it: each commitment answers the question you would ask of that artifact. Of the whole backlog: where is it heading? (Product Goal). Of this Sprint's plan: what is it for? (Sprint Goal). Of the working product: is it good enough to ship? (Definition of Done). "Without its commitment, it is just a list."

questions.stem_md: The habit-tracker group starts a Sprint with nine items taken from the Product Backlog and no Sprint Goal. At the Daily on day 5, three items are half finished and two have not been started. Someone asks whether the Sprint is going well, and nobody can say. In session 4's terms, what is missing?

options.text_md: More items in the Sprint Backlog, so nobody runs out of work
options.why_md: A longer list does not tell anyone whether the Sprint is on track; it makes the problem worse.

options.text_md: A longer Daily, so every item can be discussed in detail
options.why_md: The Daily is time-boxed to fifteen minutes; more talk does not supply the missing goal.

options.text_md: The Sprint Backlog's commitment: without a Sprint Goal it is just a list
options.why_md: The Daily's question is "Are we on track for the Sprint Goal?"; with no goal there is nothing to be on track for.

options.text_md: A Definition of Done, since half-finished items show the bar is missing
options.why_md: The DoD says when one item is done; it cannot say whether the Sprint as a whole is succeeding.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 8 pairs the Sprint Backlog with the Sprint Goal and warns that "without its commitment, it is just a list." The Daily's question is "Are we on track for the Sprint Goal?" With no goal, nine items are just nine items: nobody can tell which matter most, which could be dropped, or whether the Sprint is succeeding. A Sprint Goal such as "a user can record a habit and see this week's record" would let the team answer at once and focus the half-finished work on it.

questions.stem_md: A start-up's product manager asks the team to spend Refinement writing detailed specifications and hour estimates for all 35 items in the Product Backlog, so that she can tell customers when the last of them will ship. What does session 4 say?

options.text_md: A good use of Refinement: precise estimates for every item make the delivery dates reliable
options.why_md: That is Waterfall's assumption: a plan written in detail before anything is built, on estimates nobody can make.

options.text_md: Fine, provided it fits within Refinement's four-hour time-box
options.why_md: The time-box limits the meeting; it does not make detailing the bottom of the backlog useful. The work is waste at any length.

options.text_md: The Scrum Master should write the estimates, so the Developers can keep building
options.why_md: Moving the waste to another person does not remove it: the bottom items will still change before they are built.

options.text_md: Detail only the items near the top: the lower ones will change before they are built
options.why_md: Slide 9: estimating far-down items precisely is waste, because they will change before they are built. Slide 14 adds that Scrum makes no promise about version 1.0 a year out.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 9: the Product Backlog is "refined continuously, in detail only near the top", and "estimating item 40 precisely is waste: it will change before it is built." Slide 14 adds that Scrum gives "no promise about what is in version 1.0, a year out". The backlog is emergent: by the time the last items reach the top, the team and its users will have learned things that change them. The backlog brief applies the same rule to your group: only the top three items need detail.

questions.stem_md: The backlog brief asks for items in the shape `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>`. What job does the "so that" part do?

options.text_md: It tells the Developers how to implement the item
options.why_md: How is the Developers' decision; an item describes an outcome, not an implementation.

options.text_md: It states the benefit, which stops you building something nobody needs
options.why_md: The brief's own words: the "so that" is "the part that stops you building something nobody needs".

options.text_md: It names the test that will prove the item is done
options.why_md: Tests are part of the Definition of Done for every item; the "so that" says why a user wants it.

options.text_md: It is optional wording that makes the item sound more professional
options.why_md: The brief singles it out as the part that stops you building something nobody needs; without a benefit nobody can judge the item's value or its place in the order.

questions.explanation_md: The brief: "The 'so that' is the part that stops you building something nobody needs." Writing the benefit forces the question "who gains what?" If you cannot finish the sentence, the item probably has no value. It also helps the Product Owner order the backlog by value, because the benefit is written next to each item. Example from the expense tracker: "As a user, I can add an expense from the command line, so that I do not edit a CSV by hand."

questions.stem_md: A group's backlog starts with "Do the CSV part". According to the backlog brief, why is this not usable as an item?

options.text_md: It is too small to deserve its own entry in the backlog
options.why_md: Size is not the problem: items should be small enough to finish in a sitting. This one is vague, not small.

options.text_md: It names a file format, which belongs in the design, not in the backlog
options.why_md: Nothing in the brief keeps formats out of items; its own example "so that I do not edit a CSV by hand" names one. The problem is that it is a task.

options.text_md: It is a task, not an outcome, so nobody can tell when it is done
options.why_md: The brief's exact reason for this example.

options.text_md: Reading and writing files belongs in the Definition of Done
options.why_md: The DoD holds standards every item meets (a green check, a test, a README line), not a piece of functionality.

questions.explanation_md: The brief lists "Do the CSV part" as its first non-item: "A task, not an outcome. Nobody can tell when it is done." An item says what a user can do afterwards. Which part of the CSV: reading, writing, validating? Slide 30's rewrite answers that: "A user can add an expense and see it in the next report." That version can be checked by running the program: add an expense, run the report, see it there.

questions.stem_md: The parking-lot group (topic: spaces, tickets, duration-based pricing) drafts its Product Backlog. Sort each line into what it is.

categories.label: A standard: belongs in the Definition of Done

items.text_md: As an attendant, I can issue a ticket for a plate number, so that I know which car is in which space
items.why_md: An outcome a user gets, with a benefit, and you can check it by issuing a ticket.

items.text_md: As a driver, I can see the price of my stay when I leave, so that I pay the right amount
items.why_md: A user, an action, a benefit, and a result you can check by running the program.

items.text_md: As a manager, I can see today's takings, so that I can close the till without counting tickets by hand
items.why_md: An outcome for a real user of a parking lot, with its benefit stated.

items.text_md: Do the database part
items.why_md: Work the team does, not something a user can do afterwards; nobody can tell when it is done.

items.text_md: Set up the pricing module
items.why_md: Describes code to write, not the outcome. The outcome is a driver seeing the right price.

items.text_md: Refactor `cli.py`
items.why_md: A refactoring changes structure without changing behaviour, so no user gets anything new from it.

items.text_md: Write tests
items.why_md: The brief's own example: every item is tested, so it is a standard, not a backlog entry.

items.text_md: Make the code good
items.why_md: Not checkable as an item; quality is the bar every item meets, to be written in the DoD as something checkable.

items.text_md: The README is updated for every new command
items.why_md: A rule for every item; the brief's starter DoD has "The README says how to use the new behaviour".

questions.explanation_md: The brief's test for an item: an outcome a user gets, small enough to finish in a sitting, and you can tell when it is done, in the shape `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>`. Tasks describe work the team does ("Do the database part", "Set up the pricing module", "Refactor `cli.py`"); they may be steps inside an item, but they are not items. Standards that apply to every item ("Write tests", "Make the code good", README updated) belong in the Definition of Done.

questions.stem_md:
The gradebook group's backlog, top first:

1. As a teacher, I can see the output in colour, so that it looks nicer
2. As a teacher, I can export grades to PDF, so that I can print them
3. As a teacher, I can compute a student's weighted average, so that I can give a final grade
4. As a teacher, I can set grade boundaries, so that averages turn into letter grades

They put colour first "because it is the quickest to get working". What is wrong with the order?

options.text_md: Nothing: quick wins first build momentum for the harder items
options.why_md: The slide rules this out explicitly. Momentum on colour gives the teacher nothing they need.

options.text_md: PDF export belongs at the top, because printing is what teachers do with grades
options.why_md: Export of what? There are no averages to print until item 3 exists; its value depends on the core.

options.text_md: Grade boundaries belong at the top, because they are needed before any average
options.why_md: Boundaries turn an average into a letter; without averages they have nothing to work on.

options.text_md: The weighted average should go first: value decides the order, not ease
options.why_md: Slide 30: ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start. The weighted average is the core value; the other items depend on it.

questions.explanation_md: Session 4, slide 30: "Ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start." The top of the backlog is what you build next, so it should be the item that gives a user the most value soonest. For a gradebook, that is computing the weighted average: without it, colour, PDF export and grade boundaries have nothing to show, print or convert. Colour is not wrong to want; it is wrong to build first.

questions.stem_md: Slide 30 replaces the item "Make it good" with "Invalid input prints a message and exits non-zero". The brief's starter Definition of Done has a similar line: "Bad input prints a message and exits non-zero". What do these versions have that "Make it good" lacks?

options.text_md: They name the person in the group who is responsible for the quality of the code
options.why_md: Neither names anyone; the self-managing team decides who does what.

options.text_md: They can be checked: run it with bad input, then read the message and exit code
options.why_md: Both describe one observable behaviour with a yes-or-no answer.

options.text_md: They describe how the error handling should be implemented with typer in the code
options.why_md: They say nothing about how. They describe what a user sees, which leaves the implementation to the Developers.

options.text_md: They promise the program never crashes, which is what "good" means
options.why_md: They promise one specific behaviour, not the absence of all problems; "never crashes" would be a wish again.

questions.explanation_md: "Make it good" is not checkable: nobody can run anything and answer yes or no. "Invalid input prints a message and exits non-zero" is: run `uv run <your-app>` with bad input, read the message, then `echo $?` shows a number other than 0. Session 5 explains why that number matters: "A program that prints an error and exits 0 is a program that lies." The brief's rule for the Definition of Done ("things you can check, not things you can hope") is the same rule that makes an item usable.
questions.source_ref: S4 slide 30; backlog brief; S5 slide 9

questions.stem_md:
The backlog brief's third worked example is "As a user, I can add an expense from the command line, so that I do not edit a CSV by hand." On a clone of the expense tracker you run:

```console
$ git log --oneline v0.1
89afbe1 (tag: v0.1) Add a README and the MIT licence
bc9ef3d Add an add command that writes to data/
2ecad20 Move the report into the package behind a typer CLI
a953d05 Turn the script into a uv package
c746d38 (tag: v0.0) Print the largest expense
6efdf9d Filter by category and ignore small amounts
3e0834f Add a script that totals expenses by category
```

Which commit delivered that item?

options.text_md: `a953d05`, because packaging the script made a command-line program possible
options.why_md: That commit changed no code; it made the script installable. No user could add anything after it.

options.text_md: `2ecad20`, because it put a typer command-line interface in front of the program
options.why_md: That commit moved the existing report behind typer. A user could report, but still had to edit the CSV by hand to add an expense.

options.text_md: `bc9ef3d`, because after it a user can run `expenses add` instead of editing the file
options.why_md: The brief says this item "Became `expenses add`", and this commit adds the `add` command.

options.text_md: `3e0834f`, because the first commit created the CSV that the item depends on
options.why_md: That commit is the brief's first worked example, a total per category. It reads the CSV; it does not add to it.

questions.explanation_md: The brief says the third item "Became `expenses add`". In the history that is `bc9ef3d Add an add command that writes to data/`, which adds an `add` command to `cli.py`. The item is the outcome a user gets; the commit is how it was delivered. The earlier commits were work that made it possible (packaging in `a953d05`, a typer CLI in `2ecad20`), but after them a user still edited the CSV by hand. That is also why "package the script" would not be a backlog item: nobody gets anything from it alone.
