questions.stem_md: Slide 10 lists five words: compiles · tested · reviewed · documented · deployable. What are they the contents of?

options.text_md: A checklist the Product Owner writes for each item, saying when that item is finished
options.why_md: That is per item. The DoD is one list, decided once, applied to every item, and the brief asks the group to write it.

options.text_md: The five stages every item passes through, in order, on the team's board
options.why_md: They are not steps in sequence but conditions an item meets together; a board tracks the work, it is not the quality bar.

options.text_md: The Definition of Done: one quality bar, applied to every Increment
options.why_md: Slide 10: the quality bar every Increment meets, decided once and applied to everything. These five words are its classic contents.

options.text_md: The Sprint Goal the team agrees at Sprint Planning
options.why_md: The Sprint Goal is what this Sprint delivers, the Sprint Backlog's commitment; it changes every Sprint.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10 defines the Definition of Done as "the quality bar every Increment meets", "decided once, applied to everything", with the classic contents "compiles · tested · reviewed · documented · deployable". The point is that it does not change per item or per Sprint: the same bar for every item is what makes "done" mean the same thing every time. The backlog brief says the same: "One list, applied to everything." An item that misses any part of it is not done.

questions.stem_md:
The library-inventory group's Sprint Review is tomorrow, and their Definition of Done includes "The CI check is green". Dani pushes the overdue-fines item and says: "It's done apart from one test. I'll fix the cap next Sprint; we can show it tomorrow." The CI log's Tests step shows (trimmed):

```text
tests/test_fines.py ...F                                                 [100%]

E       assert 15.0 == 10.0
E        +  where 15.0 = overdue_fine(30)

FAILED tests/test_fines.py::test_fine_is_capped - assert 15.0 == 10.0
========================= 1 failed, 3 passed in 0.01s ==========================
```

What follows from the Definition of Done?

options.text_md: The item is done: three of four tests pass, and the failing one is an edge case
options.why_md: There is no "mostly done". The cap is a rule the item must get right, and a red check means the DoD is not met.

options.text_md: Mark the failing test as skipped so the check goes green, then present it as done
options.why_md: The check would be green and the item still wrong, so the Review would inspect a fiction. Silencing the test defeats the bar.

options.text_md: Re-run the CI job until it passes, since a single failure may be a fluke
options.why_md: The failure is not random: `overdue_fine(30)` returns 15.0, not the capped 10.0. Re-running gives the same red.

options.text_md: The item is not done and does not ship; it is not presented as finished tomorrow
options.why_md: An item that misses the DoD is not done, and "done except for tests" is not admissible.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10: "An item that misses the Definition of Done is not done, and does not ship", and "done except for tests" is not admissible. The group's DoD says the CI check is green; it is red. The output says what is wrong: for 30 days late the function returns 15.0 where the test expects the cap, 10.0, so fines are not capped. At the Review the group should say plainly that the item is not done. Whether the test or the function is wrong is a separate question (check what the rule is meant to be), but either way the item is not done today.

questions.stem_md: Two groups hand in their Definition of Done. Group A has nine lines, including "every change is reviewed by two people" and "every function has a docstring"; by their own account they check three of them. Group B has three lines (green CI, a test for the new behaviour, README updated) and checks all three on every item. Which does the backlog brief prefer, and why?

options.text_md: Group B: three lines kept are worth more than nine lines mostly ignored
options.why_md: The brief: six items you ignore are worse than three you keep. A DoD is worth what you actually check, and ignored lines teach everyone the list is decoration.

options.text_md: Group A, because a longer list sets a higher standard for every item
options.why_md: A standard nobody meets is not a standard; it only claims one.

options.text_md: Group A, as long as the ignored lines are all checked before Demo Day
options.why_md: The DoD applies to every item, every time; checking it once at the end is "done except for" by another name.

options.text_md: Neither: the Product Owner should write the Definition of Done, not the group
options.why_md: The brief asks the group to write it ("written by you"), and the lecturer holds each group to its own.

questions.explanation_md: The brief: "Cut what you will not honour. A Definition of Done with six items you ignore is worse than three you keep." An ignored line is worse than a missing one because the list then claims a standard the work does not meet: anyone reading it is misled, and the team learns that the DoD does not mean what it says. Group B's three lines are checkable and kept, so "done" means something. Group A should cut to what it will honour, or start checking the rest.

questions.stem_md: The movie-watchlist group's Definition of Done includes "Another member of the group has read the change". On the morning of a checkpoint, one item is finished and CI is green, but nobody has read it yet. Maria says: "Just this once, we count it as done; the DoD is for normal weeks." What does session 4 imply?

options.text_md: It is done, because a green CI check is the course's Definition of Done
options.why_md: The green check is the line every group must have, not the whole of this group's DoD. Their own list has a review line, and they are held to it.

options.text_md: It is done, provided the Product Owner agrees to make an exception this one time
options.why_md: The DoD is not waived item by item, by anyone; the PO decides what and in what order, not the quality bar.

options.text_md: Not done until someone reads it: the DoD is applied to every item, every time
options.why_md: The DoD is decided once and applied to everything. No exceptions per item or per deadline; that is what "applied to everything" means.

options.text_md: It is done, and the reading can happen at the Retrospective instead
options.why_md: The Retrospective is about how the team worked, not where code gets read; "done except for review" is the same as "done except for tests".

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10: the DoD is "decided once, applied to everything", and an item that misses it "is not done, and does not ship". A deadline is exactly when the DoD matters: if it bends under pressure, it was never a bar. The green CI check is the line every group shares, but each group adds its own, and the lecturer said "I hold you to your own Definition of Done". If the group finds a line it cannot honour, the place to cut it is a Retrospective, openly, not a quiet exception on a deadline morning.

questions.stem_md: A group's Definition of Done has the line "The code is clean". Which rewrite best turns it into a line anyone in the group can answer yes or no, for every item, with the course's tools?

options.text_md: `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run ruff format --check .` both pass, as in CI
options.why_md: Two commands with a yes-or-no result, both about cleanliness (lint and formatting), and both run on every push as part of the CI check.

options.text_md: `uv run pytest` passes on the author's laptop before every push
options.why_md: A useful line, but it checks behaviour, not the cleanliness this line was about, and only on one laptop.

options.text_md: `uv run ruff check .` passes on the whole project once, the day before each Review
options.why_md: Once per Sprint is not "applied to everything": an item pushed mid-Sprint is never checked, and the formatting half of "clean" is left out.

options.text_md: The Scrum Master reads each change and signs off that the code is clean
options.why_md: The Scrum Master is not an approver, and "clean" in one person's opinion is still not a yes-or-no check.

questions.explanation_md: The brief: "Write it as things you can check, not things you can hope", and session 4: "A Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish." Session 6 gave you the tools that turn "clean" into a check: `ruff check` reports lint problems and `ruff format --check` reports unformatted files, and both already run in the course's CI check on every push. The other rewrites each lose something: the tests check behaviour, not cleanliness; a check once per Sprint is not applied to every item; a sign-off is still one person's opinion. A tool cannot judge every name, so a line such as "another member has read the change" can sit beside it.
questions.source_ref: Backlog brief; S4 slide 17; S3 CI referee; S6 ruff check/format

questions.stem_md:
Joan finished the gradebook's weighted-average item. Before pushing she ran `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run pytest`, and both passed. The CI check is red at the Formatting step. You run that step's command locally:

```console
$ uv run ruff format --check .
unformatted: File would be reformatted
 --> src/gradebook/report.py:3:17
  |
2 |     total_weight = sum(weights)
  -     return sum(m*w for m,w in zip(marks, weights, strict=True)) / total_weight
3 +     return sum(m * w for m, w in zip(marks, weights, strict=True)) / total_weight
  |

1 file would be reformatted, 2 files already formatted
```

The group's Definition of Done starts with "The CI check is green". Joan says the item is done because "it passes on my machine". What is the right call?

options.text_md: Not done: run `ruff format`, commit and push, and wait for a green check
options.why_md: The referee says red, and the output names the file and line to fix. The item counts as done once the check is green.

options.text_md: Done: `ruff check` passed on Joan's machine, so the red check is GitHub's problem
options.why_md: Joan ran a different command. CI also runs `ruff format --check`, and it fails on her machine too, as shown.

options.text_md: Done: spacing around `*` is cosmetic, so it is not part of the quality bar
options.why_md: The group chose a green check as its bar; whether one step feels cosmetic does not matter. Red means not done.

options.text_md: Re-run the CI job until it goes green, then count it as done
options.why_md: The file really is unformatted, so every run gives the same red. Only changing the file fixes it.

questions.explanation_md: The course's Definition of Done is a green CI check, "the referee": the same steps for every group, on a machine none of you owns. Here it is red, so the item is not done, whatever passed on Joan's laptop. The output says exactly why: `ruff format --check` would reformat line 3 of `src/gradebook/report.py` (spaces around `*` and after the comma). Joan ran the linter, `ruff check`, but not the formatter's check. The scaffold lab's troubleshooting table gives the same fix for a red Formatting step: run `ruff format`, then commit the result.
questions.source_ref: S4 slides 10, 16; S3 slide 3; labs/01-scaffold.md troubleshooting

questions.stem_md: The meal-planner group drafts its Definition of Done. Sort each line.

categories.label: Not a DoD line: a backlog item

items.text_md: The CI check is green
items.why_md: Yes or no on the Actions tab; the line every group must have.

items.text_md: `uv sync && uv run meal-planner --help` works from a clean clone
items.why_md: Anyone can run it in an empty folder and see the result.

items.text_md: There is at least one test for the new behaviour
items.why_md: You can point at the test, or not.

items.text_md: Another member of the group has read the change
items.why_md: A fact about each change that the group can verify.

items.text_md: Bad input prints a message and exits non-zero
items.why_md: Run it with bad input and look at the message and the exit code.

items.text_md: The code is clean and easy to read
items.why_md: Nobody can answer yes or no; it needs rewriting as something checkable (for example, ruff passes).

items.text_md: We try our best to test edge cases
items.why_md: "Try our best" can never be false, so it checks nothing.

items.text_md: The program is user-friendly
items.why_md: Friendly to whom, measured how? A hope, not a check.

items.text_md: As a cook, I can scale a recipe to six servings, so that I buy the right amounts
items.why_md: An outcome a user gets: it belongs in the Product Backlog and must meet the DoD.

items.text_md: As a cook, I can get a shopping list for the week, so that I shop once
items.why_md: Another outcome for a user, so a backlog item, not part of the quality bar.

questions.explanation_md: A DoD line must apply to every item and be answerable yes or no by someone who was not in the room. The five checkable lines here come from the brief's starter list. "Clean", "try our best" and "user-friendly" are hopes: nobody can check them, and "a Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish". The two "As a cook" lines are outcomes a user gets: they belong in the Product Backlog, and the DoD is the bar each of them must meet.

questions.stem_md: Sort each statement into the ceremony it belongs to.

items.text_md: The PO and the Developers discuss implementation details of the items near the top
items.why_md: Refinement's question on slide 11; it is where the top of the backlog gets its detail.

items.text_md: The team agrees what will be delivered at the end of the Sprint
items.why_md: Sprint Planning's question on slide 11.

items.text_md: The team picks the items for the Sprint and agrees its Sprint Goal
items.why_md: What the Sprint will deliver is settled at Planning, by the team.

items.text_md: Are we on track for the Sprint Goal?
items.why_md: The Daily's question, asked every day.

items.text_md: Each developer: latest work, what next, any blockers
items.why_md: Slide 12's shape for the Daily, about a minute each.

items.text_md: Stakeholders see what was built and give feedback that changes the backlog
items.why_md: The Review is about the product: what was built, what should change.

items.text_md: At the end of the Sprint, stakeholders who tried the report say it confuses them, and the PO moves a fix up the backlog
items.why_md: Feedback changing the backlog is the point of the Review.

items.text_md: How did the team work, and what should it improve?
items.why_md: The Retrospective's question on slide 11.

items.text_md: The team agrees to run the four checks locally before every push from now on
items.why_md: A change to how the team works is a Retrospective outcome.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 11 gives each ceremony its question: Refinement, the PO and Developers discuss implementation details; Sprint Planning, agree what will be delivered; Daily, are we on track for the Sprint Goal; Review, what was built and what should change; Retrospective, how the team worked and what to improve. The two end-of-Sprint ceremonies need the most care: anything about the product and the backlog is the Review; anything about the team's way of working is the Retrospective.

questions.stem_md: Session 4 gives time-boxes for a two-week Sprint. A team moves to one-week Sprints. Roughly how long should its Sprint Review be?

options.text_md: About 30 minutes, half of the two-week time-box
options.why_md: Shorter Sprint, proportionally shorter events: half the Sprint, about half the Review.

options.text_md: One hour, since time-boxes do not depend on Sprint length
options.why_md: The slide says the opposite: events scale with the Sprint.

options.text_md: About two hours, since shorter Sprints need more feedback each time
options.why_md: Shorter Sprints get feedback more often, in shorter Reviews, not longer ones.

options.text_md: Fifteen minutes, the same time-box as the Daily
options.why_md: The Daily's fifteen minutes is a different ceremony; halving one hour gives about thirty.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 11: Sprint Review 1h for a two-week Sprint, and "Shorter Sprint → proportionally shorter events. Longer Sprint → proportionally longer events." Half the Sprint length gives about half the Review: thirty minutes. The time-box is a maximum sized to how much there is to inspect, and a one-week Sprint produces about half as much. The same rule gives a one-week Sprint about two hours of Refinement and half-hour Planning and Retrospective.

questions.stem_md:
Read this Daily Scrum of the task-manager group (two-week Sprint):

> **Head of IT** (not on the team): Right, status reports please, one by one.
>
> **Ana:** Yesterday I finished the `add` command. Today I start on due dates. No blockers.
>
> **Pol:** I'm stuck: CI fails on the lockfile and I can't push.
>
> **Head of IT:** Explain the lockfile issue in detail so I can decide who fixes it.
>
> *(twenty-five minutes of discussion between Pol and the Head of IT)*
>
> **Head of IT:** Good. Marc, you fix Pol's problem today; the rest of you carry on.

Which statement identifies what is wrong, in session 4's terms?

options.text_md: The Scrum Master, not the Head of IT, should have collected the reports and picked who helps Pol
options.why_md: That only swaps one manager for another. The Daily is not a status report to anyone, and who does what belongs to the team.

options.text_md: Pol should not have raised a blocker in front of someone senior
options.why_md: Blockers are one of the three things every developer states; hiding them breaks transparency.

options.text_md: It turned into a status report to an outsider who assigned work, and it overran its 15 minutes
options.why_md: Three rules broken at once: the Daily is not a status report to a manager, who does what belongs to the team, and the time-box is fifteen minutes.

options.text_md: Nothing serious: when a real blocker comes up, the Daily is where the team should solve it
options.why_md: A blocker is stated in a sentence at the Daily; solving it happens afterwards, with whoever the team chooses. The Daily is time-boxed to fifteen minutes.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 12: "Daily Scrum is not a status report to a manager. Fifteen minutes, for the Developers." Here an outsider runs it, asks for "status reports", and then decides who fixes Pol's problem, which breaks slide 7 too: "The team decides how the work is done, and who does what." Twenty-five minutes on the lockfile blows the time-box. The right shape is Ana's: latest work, next work, blockers. Pol's blocker should take one sentence, then be solved afterwards by whoever the team chooses, with the Scrum Master removing the impediment if it needs outside help.

questions.stem_md: At the Sprint Review, the vending-machine group runs a polished demo of change-making. The stakeholders clap, say "great job" and leave after ten minutes. Nobody comments on the product, and the Product Backlog is exactly as it was. What does session 4 say is missing?

options.text_md: A longer demo, so that the stakeholders see every feature
options.why_md: A longer show is still a show; what is missing is the stakeholders' feedback.

options.text_md: Feedback from the stakeholders that changes what is in the Product Backlog
options.why_md: Slide 12: the Review is not a demo for applause; stakeholders come to give feedback and change the backlog.

options.text_md: A discussion of how the team worked during the Sprint
options.why_md: That is the Retrospective's question; the Review is about the product.

options.text_md: The stakeholders' formal sign-off that the Increment meets the Definition of Done
options.why_md: The DoD is a checkable bar the team applies itself (with the CI check), not something stakeholders approve at the Review.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 12: "Review is not a demo for applause. Stakeholders come to give feedback and change the backlog." Slide 11's question for the Review has two halves: "What was built; what should change". This Review answered the first half and skipped the second. A Review that leaves the backlog untouched wastes the one meeting where users and stakeholders can redirect the product. Asking them what confused them, or what they want next, is the point of the meeting.

questions.stem_md: At the end of a Sprint, the parking-lot group realises that pushes collided all Sprint because nobody had agreed who pushes when. They agree a rule: announce in the group chat before pushing to `main`. In which ceremony does this conversation belong?

options.text_md: The Sprint Review, because it happens at the end of the Sprint
options.why_md: Both end-of-Sprint ceremonies happen then. The Review is about the product and the backlog, not the team's way of working.

options.text_md: The Daily, because colliding pushes are a blocker that the developers must raise
options.why_md: A collision on one day is a blocker to mention at the Daily; a rule changing how the team works from now on is a Retrospective outcome.

options.text_md: Refinement, because it changes how items will be implemented
options.why_md: Refinement details backlog items with the PO; a push rule is not about any item.

options.text_md: The Sprint Retrospective: it is about how the team works and what to change
options.why_md: Slide 11's question for the Retrospective: how the team worked, and what to improve.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 11: the Retrospective answers "How the team worked, and what to improve", and slide 12 adds that it is about "what worked and what did not, and what changes can be introduced accordingly". A push rule is a change to how the team works. The Review asks a different question, "What was built; what should change", about the product. Notice also the absence of blame: the problem is framed as a missing agreement, not as whose push broke things. The scaffold lab gave the same advice: agree who pushes when.

questions.stem_md: Which description of the shape of a Scrum team matches session 4?

options.text_md: Any size, as long as a team lead assigns work to each specialist
options.why_md: A lead handing out work breaks two rules: hierarchy stays horizontal, and the team decides who does what.

options.text_md: At least fifteen people, so that every skill is covered inside the team
options.why_md: Cross-functional, yes, but ideally ten people or fewer; a bigger group needs splitting, not growing.

options.text_md: A Scrum Master at the top, managing the Product Owner and the Developers
options.why_md: The Scrum Master is "not a manager": the role ensures the process works and coaches.

options.text_md: Ideally ten people or fewer, with hierarchy kept as horizontal as possible
options.why_md: Both lines are on slide 6, under the table of accountabilities.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6, under the table of accountabilities: "The team should ideally consist of ten people or fewer. Hierarchy stays as horizontal as possible." The three accountabilities sit side by side: the PO decides what and in what order, the Developers decide how and who, and the Scrum Master ensures the process works without managing anyone. Cross-functional means the skills to finish an item are inside the team, which is a reason to choose people well, not to grow the team past ten.

questions.stem_md: The task-manager group's board shows every item of the Sprint in the Done column. At the Sprint Review everyone looks at the board and is pleased. In fact half the items fail the CI check, and the group knew. Which pillar has failed, and what does the Review end up doing?

options.text_md: Adaptation: the group saw a problem and did not change course, so the next Sprint repeats this one
options.why_md: Nothing was changed because nothing was shown. The problem never reached the Review, so there was no inspection to adapt to. (Slide 13's line for this: "Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times.")

options.text_md: Transparency: the board hides the real state, so the Review inspects a fiction, not the product
options.why_md: The Review inspected a board that hid the real state of the product. Slide 13: "Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction."

options.text_md: The Definition of Done: it could not be checked, so nobody knew which items failed
options.why_md: Their Definition of Done was checkable: CI told them the items failed, and they knew. The board hid what the check said. (Slide 10: "A Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish.")

options.text_md: Estimation: the items were planned too precisely and so could not meet the check
options.why_md: The story is about hiding the state of finished work, not about planning future work in too much detail.

questions.explanation_md: Scrum's pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation, in that order for a reason: you can only inspect what is visible, and only adapt to what you inspected. A board that says Done while the CI check is red makes the Review inspect the board, not the product. Session 4's line names it: "Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction." The Definition of Done exists to prevent exactly this: an item that fails it is not done and should never reach the Done column.

questions.stem_md: For four Sprints in a row, the habit-tracker group's Retrospective notes the same problem: people push without running the tests, and CI goes red. Everyone agrees it is a problem. Nobody proposes a change, because it would mean telling two teammates that their habit has to stop. Which value is missing, according to session 4?

options.text_md: Courage: the problem is seen and named, but nobody acts on it
options.why_md: Slide 13: adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times. The problem is seen and named; acting on it needs courage.

options.text_md: Focus: the team is spread across too many items to fix anything
options.why_md: Nothing suggests the team works on too much at once; the problem is seen and named, then not acted on.

options.text_md: Openness: the team hides the problem from itself
options.why_md: The problem is raised openly at every Retrospective. What is missing is the will to act on it.

options.text_md: Respect: the team should not comment on teammates' habits
options.why_md: Respect does not mean avoiding hard conversations; a Retrospective is about what changes, not blame, and that requires saying it.

questions.explanation_md: Session 4: "Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times." The team inspects (the Retrospective names the problem) but never adapts, because adapting means an uncomfortable conversation. Courage is the value that turns an observation into a change, for example agreeing that everyone runs `ruff`, `mypy` and `pytest` locally before pushing. Because the Retrospective is not blame, the change can be framed as a team rule rather than an accusation.

questions.stem_md: A client asks what adopting Scrum will give her project. Which one of these does Scrum actually provide?

options.text_md: A requirements document agreed before development starts
options.why_md: Slide 14 lists it first under what Scrum does not give you; the backlog is emergent instead.

options.text_md: A testing strategy and engineering practices for the code
options.why_md: Scrum gives "no architecture, no testing strategy, no engineering practices at all"; the course takes those from XP.

options.text_md: A promise of what will be in version 1.0, a year out
options.why_md: Explicitly not given: the backlog changes as everyone learns.

options.text_md: Short time-boxed Sprints, each ending with an Increment to inspect
options.why_md: That is the organisation Scrum supplies: rhythm, roles, an ordered backlog, a working Increment.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 14: no requirements document; no promise about what is in version 1.0, a year out; no architecture, no testing strategy, no engineering practices at all. "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it." What it does give is the organisation: three accountabilities, an ordered backlog, Sprints with time-boxed ceremonies, and an Increment meeting a Definition of Done at the end of each. How the code is built well (tests, CI, clean code) has to come from elsewhere.

questions.stem_md: A student says: "The course isn't real Scrum. It uses Scrum's words, but the engineering comes from XP (TDD, CI, small commits) and we track work on a Kanban board." Which reply fits sessions 2 and 4 best?

options.text_md: Scrum gives no engineering practices, so borrowing XP's fills that gap
options.why_md: Session 4 names the gap; session 2 names the principle of borrowing the practices that help you iterate fast and deliver value.

options.text_md: True, so the project should drop the XP practices and keep to the ceremonies
options.why_md: Ceremonies alone are the mistake slide 14 warns about: following them is not enough to get real work done.

options.text_md: True, so the course should pick one methodology and follow it exactly
options.why_md: Session 2 says the opposite: it is not about picking one methodology and following blindly.

options.text_md: Not true: Scrum already includes TDD and CI, so the course is plain Scrum
options.why_md: Slide 14: Scrum gives no engineering practices at all. TDD and CI come from XP (session 2), which is why the course borrows them.

questions.explanation_md: Session 4, slide 14: Scrum gives "no architecture, no testing strategy, no engineering practices at all". Something has to fill that gap, and session 2 named it: "XP's engineering practices are the technical spine: TDD, CI, small commits", with a Kanban board to track the group's work. Session 2's closing principle: "It is not about picking one methodology and following blindly, but borrowing the practices that will help you iterate fast and deliver value."

questions.stem_md: Session 4 mapped Scrum onto the course. Which pairing is right?

options.text_md: Product Owner → your group's most experienced member
options.why_md: The PO in the course is the lecturer; your group are the Developers.

options.text_md: Sprint → one Tuesday or Friday session
options.why_md: A Sprint is the stretch between two checkpoints, which spans several sessions.

options.text_md: Sprint Review → practice sessions and Demo Day
options.why_md: Where the working product is shown and gets feedback, as in a Review.

options.text_md: Definition of Done → the lecturer's view of your code
options.why_md: The DoD is a green CI check, the same for every group: a referee, not an opinion.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 16's table: Sprint = the stretch between two checkpoints; Sprint Goal = the checkpoint's deliverable; Definition of Done = a green CI check, the same one for all groups; Product Owner = the lecturer; Developers = your group; Sprint Review = practice sessions and Demo Day. The practice sessions and Demo Day are where the working product is shown and gets feedback, which is what a Review is for.

questions.stem_md: Using session 4's mapping, what was the Sprint Goal of the Sprint that ended on Friday 25 September (session 5)?

options.text_md: Attending the practice session and getting feedback from the lecturer
options.why_md: The practice session is where the Review happens; the goal is what the Sprint delivers.

options.text_md: Checkpoint 1's deliverable: the scaffold with one real command, at `v0.1`
options.why_md: The Sprint Goal is the checkpoint's deliverable, and CP1 was marked at the `v0.1` tag.

options.text_md: Writing at least eight backlog items and a Definition of Done for the topic
options.why_md: That was the session 4 workshop, handed in the same day; the Sprint's deliverable was the scaffold at `v0.1`.

options.text_md: A finished program a stranger can run from the container image
options.why_md: That is the final submission and Demo Day; the first Sprint's goal was much smaller.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 16 maps the Sprint to "the stretch between two checkpoints" and the Sprint Goal to "the checkpoint's deliverable". CP1 was marked at the `v0.1` tag on 25 September: in session 5's words, the repository "stops being a template and becomes the home for your project", with one command of your own. Its Definition of Done was CP1's three binary items: the clean-clone `--help` check, the `src/` layout with an importable package, and a README that says what the program does and how to run it.

questions.stem_md:
On Marta's laptop, `uv run parking --help` works. Before tagging `v0.1`, the group checks CP1 item 1 the way the scaffold lab says: they clone the repository into an empty folder, `/tmp/cp1`, and run there:

```console
$ uv sync && uv run parking --help
Using CPython 3.13.15
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 9 packages in 3ms
Installed 8 packages in 7ms
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/cp1/.venv/bin/parking", line 4, in <module>
    from parking_lot.cli import app
  File "/tmp/cp1/src/parking_lot/cli.py", line 3, in <module>
    from parking_lot.pricing import price_for
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'parking_lot.pricing'
```

What should the group conclude?

options.text_md: The clean clone is at fault: it works on Marta's laptop, so item 1 is already met
options.why_md: Item 1 says "from a clean clone" because the laptop is not the test. It works there only because the file exists there.

options.text_md: `pricing.py` is missing from the repository: commit and push it before item 1 counts
options.why_md: The clone has every pushed file and nothing else, so a module missing there is missing from the repository.

options.text_md: Delete `.venv` and run `uv sync` again, since the environment did not install the module
options.why_md: The environment installed fine. No reinstall can create a file the repository does not have.

options.text_md: Add `parking_lot.pricing` to the dependencies in `pyproject.toml` and sync again
options.why_md: It is the group's own module, not a package from PyPI; dependencies are for other people's code.

questions.explanation_md: The clean clone did its job. `uv sync` worked, but `cli.py` imports `parking_lot.pricing` and the clone has no such module. On Marta's laptop the file exists, so everything runs there. `git status` on her machine says which mistake it was: `src/parking_lot/pricing.py` under "Untracked files" (never committed), or a branch "ahead of 'origin/main'" (committed, never pushed). The lab explains why CP1 is checked this way: a clean clone "has no `.venv`, no caches and nothing you forgot to commit", so it catches the file that only exists on your laptop. Until the file is committed and pushed, item 1 of this binary Definition of Done is not met.

questions.stem_md: The project brief calls the automated CI check "the referee, not the judge". What does that mean for a checkpoint submission?

options.text_md: Red means not mechanically valid; the checklist or rubric gives the marks
options.why_md: The brief: "it is not marked itself, but a red check means the submission is not mechanically valid". The marks come from the checklist or the rubric.

options.text_md: The check gives the mark, so a green check on the tag means full marks
options.why_md: The check is not marked itself. Green makes a submission valid; it does not make it good.

options.text_md: The check is advisory, so a red check is ignored if the lecturer likes the code
options.why_md: Red means not mechanically valid; for the partial, red at `v0.5` caps Tests at 1.

options.text_md: The check only runs on the lecturer's own machine on the deadline day
options.why_md: It runs on GitHub on every push, on a machine none of you owns, so you can see it before submitting.

questions.explanation_md: The project brief: an automated check runs on every push and must be green; "it is not marked itself, but a red check means the submission is not mechanically valid. Think of it as the referee, not the judge." A referee enforces the same rules for everyone; the judge (the checklist or rubric, applied by the lecturer) decides how good the work is. That is why the course's Definition of Done is a green check: public, binary, the same for all groups and checkable before you submit.
questions.source_ref: Project brief (moodle/project-pages.md); partial rubric; S4 slides 16–17

questions.stem_md: The gradebook group tags `v0.5` on Sunday at 21:00; CI on that commit is red at the Types step. At 23:00 they push a fix to `main`, CI goes green on the new commit, and they go to bed without touching the tag. What does the marker look at after the 23:59 deadline?

options.text_md: The green commit, because `main` is what counts at the deadline
options.why_md: The rubric marks `main` at the `v0.5` tag, which still points at the red commit.

options.text_md: The red commit, but CI results are not considered for the partial
options.why_md: The rubric's CI gate says the opposite: red at `v0.5` caps the Tests criterion at 1.

options.text_md: The red commit at the tag, so the Tests criterion is capped at 1
options.why_md: The partial is marked at the `v0.5` tag, and the CI gate looks at that commit: that Increment misses the Definition of Done.

options.text_md: Nothing at all, because the tag became invalid when `main` moved on
options.why_md: A tag is a permanent name for one commit; it is still there, pointing at the wrong commit.

questions.explanation_md: The rubric: the partial is "marked against your group repo's main at the `v0.5` tag", the check must be green on that commit, and "a fix pushed after the tag does not count: move the tag, or tag again as `v0.5` before the deadline." The scaffold lab defines a tag as "a permanent name for one commit". In Scrum terms, the Increment the group submitted is the one at the tag, and it misses the Definition of Done. Moving the tag onto the green commit before 23:59 would have made the green Increment the one that counts.

questions.stem_md:
The parking-lot group (topic: "spaces, tickets, duration-based pricing") hands in this Product Backlog, top first:

1. Make the output look good with colours
2. Do the database part
3. Write tests for pricing
4. Pricing
5. As an attendant, I can issue a ticket for a plate number, so that I know which car is in which space
6. Make the code good

parts.prompt_md: Pick two lines other than 5 and say, for each, why it is not usable as a backlog item.
parts.model_answer_md: "Do the database part" is a task, not an outcome: nobody can tell when it is done. "Write tests for pricing" is a standard every item meets, so it belongs in the Definition of Done.
rubric: Identifies a line as a task or topic rather than an outcome (2 or 4) and says nobody can tell when it is done or no user gets anything
Identifies a line as a standard for every item (3 or 6) that belongs in the Definition of Done
Identifies a line as not checkable or with no stated benefit (1 or 6)
parts.weak_answers_md: "They are too vague" or "badly written" without the reason scores nothing: name it (task not outcome, standard not item, not checkable). Saying "Write tests for pricing" should be deleted misses that tests still matter: they move to the Definition of Done. Saying "Pricing" is too short misses the real issue: it names a topic, not what a user can do.

parts.prompt_md: Rewrite two of the lines, in words, as usable items in the brief's shape.
parts.model_answer_md: Line 4: "As a driver, I can see the price of my stay when I leave, so that I pay the right amount." Line 2: "As an attendant, I can reopen the program and still see today's tickets, so that no car is lost overnight."
rubric: Each rewrite follows the shape `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>`, with a real user of a parking lot (driver, attendant, manager)
Each rewrite is an outcome you can check by running the program, with a real benefit in the "so that"
parts.weak_answers_md: A rewrite that keeps the task ("As a developer, I can set up the database, so that data is stored") only changes the wording: the user is the team itself and nothing is checkable from outside. Dropping the "so that" loses the part that stops you building something nobody needs. Rewriting "Write tests" as an item misses that it belongs in the DoD.

parts.prompt_md: Which item should be at the top, and why? Why do only the top three need detail?
parts.model_answer_md: Issuing a ticket goes first: it is the parking lot's core value, and colours give nobody anything; order by value, not ease. Only the top three need detail because the rest will change before they are built.
rubric: Puts a core outcome first (issuing a ticket or pricing a stay) and justifies it by value, not ease
Says the lower items will change before they are built, so detailing or estimating them now is waste
parts.weak_answers_md: Keeping colours first "because it is quick" is the mistake slide 30 names: ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start. Saying the top three get detail "because the PO says so" or "to save time" misses the reason: the backlog is emergent and the rest will change before anyone builds it.

questions.explanation_md: The brief's test for an item is an outcome a user gets, small enough to finish in a sitting, that you can tell is done, written as `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>`. Lines 2 and 4 are a task and a topic, lines 3 and 6 are standards for the Definition of Done, and line 1 has no real benefit for a parking lot and should not be first: order by value, not by what is easiest to start. Only line 5 survives as it is. The order follows value: a parking lot exists to issue tickets and price stays.

questions.stem_md:
The gradebook group's Definition of Done:

1. The code is clean and readable
2. The CI check is green
3. We test as much as we can
4. `uv sync && uv run gradebook --help` works from a clean clone
5. The program is fast
6. Every function has a docstring and a test, and the whole team reviews every change
7. The README says how to use the new behaviour

By their own account, the group checks lines 2, 4 and 7 on every item and has never checked the others.

parts.prompt_md: Pick two lines that are wishes rather than checks and explain why each fails as a DoD line.
parts.model_answer_md: Lines 1 and 3. Nobody can answer yes or no to "clean and readable" or "as much as we can"; they are hopes, and a Definition of Done you cannot check yourself is a wish.
rubric: Names two of lines 1, 3 and 5 as wishes
Explains that they cannot be answered yes or no by someone else, so they are hopes, not checks
parts.weak_answers_md: Picking line 6 as a wish is a misreading: it is checkable, just ignored. Answers that say a line is "too vague" without saying why (no yes-or-no answer, nobody outside could check it) get half the marks at most.

parts.prompt_md: Rewrite one of your two lines, in words, as something the group can check.
parts.model_answer_md: Line 3 becomes "There is at least one test for the new behaviour, and the tests pass in CI".
rubric: The rewrite has a yes-or-no answer someone outside the group could check (a test exists, a tool passes, a measured time)
parts.weak_answers_md: "We test thoroughly" or "we really try to keep it clean" changes the words, not the problem: it is still a hope. A good rewrite names something you can point at or run.

parts.prompt_md: Line 6 is checkable, but the group never checks it. What does the brief advise, and why?
parts.model_answer_md: Cut it, or cut it to what they will honour, such as "another member has read the change". Six ignored lines are worse than three kept: the list claims a bar the work does not meet.
rubric: Says to cut what they will not honour, or reduce it to a part they will keep
Explains that an ignored line is worse than none: the list claims a standard that is not met and loses its meaning
parts.weak_answers_md: "Keep it, it shows ambition" is the trap the brief warns about. "Check it before Demo Day" misses that the DoD applies to every item, every time, not once at the end.

parts.prompt_md: Which line can the group not remove, and why?
parts.model_answer_md: Line 2, the green CI check: the same check for every group, on a machine none of them owns.
rubric: Names line 2 and says it is required of every group (the course's DoD, the referee)
parts.weak_answers_md: Naming line 4 confuses CP1's items with the DoD line the brief says is "not yours to choose". Saying "because the lecturer likes it" misses the reason: one public, binary check for everyone.

questions.explanation_md: The brief's rules for a DoD: "the bar every item meets. One list, applied to everything. Write it as things you can check, not things you can hope", and "Cut what you will not honour. A Definition of Done with six items you ignore is worse than three you keep." Session 4 adds that a DoD you cannot check yourself is a wish. The green CI check is the one line that is not yours to choose.

questions.stem_md: The text-adventure group is proud of its Scrum: a Daily every morning, always under fifteen minutes; Sprint Planning, Review and Retrospective on schedule; a tidy board. At the partial submission, `uv sync` fails from a clean clone, there are two tests, and CI has been red for a week. Every Retrospective concluded that "communication went well".

parts.prompt_md: Using session 4's slide on what Scrum does not give you, explain how a team can run every ceremony and still ship nothing that works.
parts.model_answer_md: Scrum organises the work; it does not do it. It gives no architecture and no testing strategy, so following the ceremonies is not enough: the code still needs tests, a lockfile that installs and a green check.
rubric: States or paraphrases "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it"
Says Scrum provides no engineering practices or testing strategy, so ceremonies alone do not produce working software
parts.weak_answers_md: "They did Scrum wrong" without saying what is missing scores little. Blaming the time-boxes or the Daily misses the point: the ceremonies ran fine, and that is exactly the slide's warning. What was absent is the engineering: tests, an install that works, a green check.

parts.prompt_md: Which part of Scrum itself did they still get wrong? Name the commitment they ignored and one pillar or value missing.
parts.model_answer_md: No Increment met the Definition of Done (a green CI check), so nothing was done, whatever the board said. The Reviews inspected a fiction (no transparency), and the Retrospectives lacked the courage to name the red check.
rubric: Names the Definition of Done (the Increment's commitment) as not met: red CI means not done
Names transparency (inspecting a fiction) or courage (the same Sprint again), linked to the story
parts.weak_answers_md: Naming a value without linking it to the story ("they lacked respect") gets no mark. Missing that a red CI check for a week means no item was done is the central gap.

parts.prompt_md: Name two changes for the next Sprint.
parts.model_answer_md: Treat the green check as the bar: nothing moves to Done while CI is red, and fixing it comes first. Adopt the XP practices the course borrows: a test for each new behaviour, the four checks run before pushing, a clean-clone check before tagging.
rubric: A change that enforces the Definition of Done (no item counts as done with CI red; fix CI first)
A concrete engineering practice (tests per behaviour, local checks before push, clean-clone check, small commits)
parts.weak_answers_md: "Have longer Retrospectives" or "add another ceremony" repeats the mistake: more organisation, no more engineering. Vague answers ("work harder", "communicate better") are not changes anyone can check. A good change is one you could verify at the next Review: CI green, a test for each item.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 14 warns of the tendency "to believe that following the ceremonies around Scrum is enough to get real work done". Scrum organises the work; the engineering practices (tests, CI, a lockfile that installs) do it, and the course takes them from XP. This group also broke Scrum itself: with CI red for a week no item met the Definition of Done, so the board and the Reviews inspected a fiction, and the Retrospectives lacked the courage to say so.

questions.stem_md:
Two scenes from the end of the flashcard-trainer group's Sprint.

**Review.** The group shows its Leitner-box feature to two classmates acting as users. The classmates say "nice". Nobody asks them anything, and the Product Backlog is unchanged afterwards.

**Retrospective.** Forty minutes are spent establishing that Iker's push broke CI on Wednesday. The meeting ends when Iker apologises. Nothing else is decided.

parts.prompt_md: What is each of these ceremonies for, according to session 4?
parts.model_answer_md: The Review asks what was built and what should change: stakeholders come to give feedback and change the backlog. The Retrospective asks how the team worked and what to improve.
rubric: Review: what was built and what should change; feedback that changes the backlog
Retrospective: how the team worked and what to improve
parts.weak_answers_md: Swapping them (the Review discusses how the team worked) is the classic confusion. "The Review is to show the work" gets half: it leaves out the feedback and the backlog change.

parts.prompt_md: What went wrong in each scene?
parts.model_answer_md: The Review became a demo for applause: no feedback was asked for, so the backlog could not change. The Retrospective became blame: it found a culprit instead of discussing what worked, what did not and what to change.
rubric: Review treated as a demo for applause: no feedback, backlog unchanged
Retrospective turned into blame, with no change agreed
parts.weak_answers_md: "The Review was too short" misses the point; a long demo is still a demo. "Iker should be more careful" repeats the blame instead of naming it as the problem.

parts.prompt_md: Suggest one concrete change for each meeting.
parts.model_answer_md: At the Review, ask the users what confused them and what they want next, and let the Product Owner reorder the backlog from their answers. At the Retrospective, ask why a broken push could reach `main` and agree a team rule, such as running the four checks locally before every push.
rubric: A Review change that produces feedback or a backlog change (ask users questions; the PO reorders)
A Retrospective change about the process, not a person (a rule such as local checks before pushing)
parts.weak_answers_md: "Iker should not push any more" is still blame, aimed at a person instead of the process. "Invite more people to the Review" does not help if nobody asks them anything, and "make the demo better" keeps the Review a show.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 11 gives the questions: the Review, "What was built; what should change"; the Retrospective, "How the team worked, and what to improve". Slide 12 adds what they are not: the Review is not a demo for applause (stakeholders give feedback and change the backlog), and the Retrospective is not blame (the team discusses what worked, what did not, and what changes to introduce).

questions.stem_md: A software company runs two-week Sprints. On day 4, the sales director, who is not on the team, walks in: "A client wants a monthly-summary report by Friday. Put it in this Sprint. Laura, you do it tonight; skip the tests, we can add them later."

parts.prompt_md: Name three things in this request that break session 4's rules, and the rule each one breaks.
parts.model_answer_md: He decides how much goes into the Sprint, but nobody outside does. He decides who does the work, but the team decides who does what. "Skip the tests" produces an item that misses the Definition of Done, and "done except for tests" is not admissible.
rubric: An outsider deciding how much goes into the Sprint (nobody outside decides)
An outsider deciding who does what or how (that belongs to the self-managing team)
Skipping tests: the item would miss the Definition of Done, so it is not done
The request bypasses the Product Owner, who decides what is worth doing and in what order
parts.weak_answers_md: Naming only the urgency ("Friday is too soon") misses the rules. "He is rude" is not a Scrum rule. Many answers find the outsider and the tests but forget that "Laura, you do it" is a decision that belongs to the team.

parts.prompt_md: What should happen to the request instead?
parts.model_answer_md: It goes to the Product Owner, who decides whether it is worth doing and where it goes in the Product Backlog. If it is urgent, the PO can put it at the top for the next Sprint Planning; only the PO could cancel the current Sprint, which almost never happens.
rubric: The request goes to the Product Owner and into the Product Backlog, ordered by value
It is picked up at the next Sprint Planning (or, rarely, the PO cancels the Sprint)
parts.weak_answers_md: "The team says no" is incomplete: the request is not rejected, it is routed to the person who orders the work. "The Scrum Master decides" gives the decision to the wrong role.

parts.prompt_md: What is the Scrum Master's part in this?
parts.model_answer_md: To make the process work: send the director to the PO and protect the Sprint from the interruption, treating it as an impediment to remove.
rubric: The Scrum Master protects the process, removing the impediment by redirecting the request to the PO, without deciding on the request
parts.weak_answers_md: "The Scrum Master assigns it to someone with time" makes the Scrum Master a manager, which the slide says the role is not. "The Scrum Master tells the director no" is closer but incomplete: the request is not rejected, it is sent to the Product Owner.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7: the team decides how the work is done and who does what; the PO decides what is worth doing and in what order; nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint. Slide 10: "done except for tests" is not admissible. Slide 6: the Scrum Master ensures the process works and removes impediments, and is not a manager. Slide 12: the PO retains the power to cancel the Sprint, and this almost never happens.

questions.stem_md:
The meal-planner group's Definition of Done:

1. The CI check is green
2. There is at least one test for the new behaviour
3. The README says how to use the new behaviour

Nico pushes a new `scale` command (recipes scaled by servings) and a README line. CI is green: all 9 existing tests pass. He adds no test and says: "CI is green, and the course's Definition of Done is a green CI check, so it's done."

parts.prompt_md: Is the item done? Explain using the group's Definition of Done.
parts.model_answer_md: No. Lines 1 and 3 are met but line 2 is not: no test covers `scale`. The DoD is one list applied to everything, and an item that misses any line is not done and does not ship.
rubric: Says not done because line 2 (a test for the new behaviour) is not met
Says the whole DoD applies to every item; missing one line means not done
parts.weak_answers_md: "Done, because CI is green" accepts Nico's argument. "Nearly done" is "done except for tests", which session 4 says is not admissible. Answers that quote line 1 and stop there miss that the DoD is the whole list, applied to every item.

parts.prompt_md: How can CI be green while the new behaviour is untested?
parts.model_answer_md: CI only runs the tests that exist. With no test for `scale`, nothing checks it, so nothing about it can fail: green says the existing tests pass, not that the new code is right.
rubric: CI runs only the existing tests; with no test for `scale`, nothing about it can fail
A green check is necessary, not sufficient: it does not show that the new behaviour works
parts.weak_answers_md: "CI must be broken" misreads it: CI did exactly its job. Answers that say "the tests are wrong" miss that the problem is a test that does not exist. A check can only fail on what it checks.

parts.prompt_md: How does the course's Definition of Done relate to the group's own?
parts.model_answer_md: The green CI check is the line every group must have; each group adds its own checkable lines, and the lecturer holds each group to its own Definition of Done.
rubric: Green CI is the shared minimum, not theirs to choose; the group's own lines add to it and bind them too
parts.weak_answers_md: "The course's DoD replaces the group's" is Nico's mistake. "The group's DoD replaces CI" is the opposite mistake: the green check is not optional. The two stack: the shared minimum, plus the group's own lines.

questions.explanation_md: The course maps the Definition of Done to a green CI check, the line that is not yours to choose; the backlog brief asks each group to add its own checkable lines, and the lecturer said "I hold you to your own Definition of Done". A green check only shows that the tests that exist pass. That is why the brief's starter list adds "There is at least one test for the new behaviour": without it, new code can arrive with nothing that could ever turn the check red.

questions.stem_md: A client wants a gym-workout logger for her chain of gyms. She asks for a signed requirements document before any code is written, and a fixed promise of what version 1.0 will contain in twelve months. You propose Scrum instead.

parts.prompt_md: What is she asking for that Scrum does not give?
parts.model_answer_md: Scrum gives no requirements document and no promise about what is in version 1.0 a year out. The Product Backlog is emergent: it is reordered and refined as everyone learns, and only the top is detailed.
rubric: No requirements document and no fixed promise for version 1.0 a year out
The backlog is emergent: it changes as the team learns, and only the top is detailed
parts.weak_answers_md: "Scrum is faster" does not answer the question. Saying Scrum gives a requirements document "in the backlog" misses that the backlog is never finished and only detailed near the top, so there is nothing to sign off up front.

parts.prompt_md: What does she get instead?
parts.model_answer_md: A working Increment every Sprint that meets the Definition of Done, a Sprint Review where she gives feedback and changes the backlog, and one Product Owner who orders the work by value.
rubric: Frequent working Increments that meet the Definition of Done
Feedback at each Review that changes the backlog, with the PO ordering by value
parts.weak_answers_md: "Flexibility" alone is too vague to score. Promising that Scrum delivers everything she wanted, sooner, is the over-sell session 2 warned about: Agile is not free. Name what she sees and when: a working Increment every Sprint, and a Review where her feedback changes the plan.

parts.prompt_md: Name one real cost of the switch for her, as session 2's workshop asked.
parts.model_answer_md: Less up-front certainty about the final scope, so it is harder to agree a fixed price for a fixed scope. She also has to spend time at Reviews giving feedback.
rubric: Names a real downside: less certainty about final scope, a harder fixed price, or her time needed at Reviews
Explains why it follows (scope emerges Sprint by Sprint; feedback needs her)
parts.weak_answers_md: "No downside" contradicts the workshop, which asked for at least one. A downside that does not follow from Scrum ("developers are lazier") scores nothing. The workshop asked for a real cost precisely because switching is never free.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 14: Scrum gives no requirements document and no promise about version 1.0 a year out; Scrum organises the work. Session 2 explains why: Waterfall's assumption of stable, known requirements fails for software, and Agile replaces it with short cycles of working software and feedback. The session 2 workshop asked groups to name what switching costs (less up-front certainty, a harder fixed price, more coordination): Agile is not free.

questions.stem_md: The movie-watchlist group books its meetings for a two-week Sprint (the Daily stays at 15 minutes). Which booking matches session 4's time-boxes?

options.text_md: Refinement 1h · Planning ~4h · Review 1h · Retrospective 1h
options.why_md: This swaps the two planning meetings. On slide 11 Refinement is the long one (~4h); Sprint Planning only has to agree what the Sprint will deliver, in 1h.

options.text_md: Refinement ~4h · Planning 1h · Review ~4h · Retrospective 1h
options.why_md: The Review is 1h for a two-week Sprint, the same as Planning and the Retrospective. The long meeting is Refinement.

options.text_md: No Refinement · Planning 1h · Review 1h · Retrospective 1h
options.why_md: Slide 11 lists Refinement as a ceremony of about four hours: it is where the items near the top of the backlog get their detail.

options.text_md: Refinement ~4h · Planning 1h · Review 1h · Retrospective 1h
options.why_md: Slide 11's time-boxes for a two-week Sprint.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 11, for a two-week Sprint: Refinement ~4h, Sprint Planning 1h, Daily 15 min, Sprint Review 1h, Sprint Retrospective 1h, and "Shorter Sprint → proportionally shorter events". The long meeting is Refinement, where the Product Owner and the Developers work through the items near the top of the backlog. With those items already detailed, Sprint Planning only has to agree what the Sprint will deliver, in an hour. Books and websites about Scrum give other maximums; the exam follows the slide.

questions.stem_md: In its first week, a team building a habit-tracking app writes 25 backlog items. The Product Owner and the Developers sign the list and agree that nothing new goes in until all 25 are built. In week 5, users trying the first Increment keep asking for a daily reminder. What does session 4 say should happen to the reminder?

options.text_md: It waits until all 25 signed items are built, so that the agreed plan holds
options.why_md: That treats the backlog as a signed specification, the Waterfall gate from session 2. Slide 9: the Product Backlog is emergent and never finished.

options.text_md: It goes on a separate list of new ideas, so that the signed backlog stays stable
options.why_md: Two lists means two orders and no single place where every request competes on value. The PO owns and orders one Product Backlog.

options.text_md: It goes into the Product Backlog, where the PO orders it by value
options.why_md: Ordered, emergent, never finished: new items appear as people use the product, and the PO decides where they go.

options.text_md: It goes at the bottom of the backlog, since items are built in the order they arrive
options.why_md: Position is a decision about value, not about arrival. Top = next because the PO put it there.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 9: the Product Backlog is "Ordered. Emergent. Never finished." New items appear as people use the product and learn, which is why Agile puts working software in front of users early. A backlog that is signed and closed is a requirements document in disguise, and slide 14 says Scrum does not give you one. The reminder goes into the one Product Backlog, and the Product Owner decides its place. If users keep asking for it, it may well go near the top.

questions.stem_md: The fare-calculator group checks Checkpoint 1 before tagging `v0.1`. From a clean clone, `uv sync && uv run fares --help` works and lists their command, and the package `fare_calculator` imports without errors. The whole README is one sentence: "A fare calculator for zones and travelcards." Which CP1 item is not met?

options.text_md: None: the README says what the program does, and both commands work
options.why_md: The README item asks for what it does and how to run it; session 5's version adds how to install. A stranger cannot get from this README to a first run.

options.text_md: The README item: it says what the program is, but not how to install and run it
options.why_md: The item is binary: the README tells a stranger how to run the program, or it does not. This one does not.

options.text_md: The clean-clone item: it works, but only for someone who already knows the command
options.why_md: The clean-clone item is the command working from a clean clone, and it does. Telling people which command to type is the README's job.

options.text_md: The layout item: a README must describe the `src/` layout before the package counts
options.why_md: The layout item is the `src/` layout with the package importable, and both are true here. It says nothing about the README.

questions.explanation_md: CP1 is a Definition of Done in miniature: three binary items, "checkable before you submit". Items 1 and 2 are met: the commands work from a clean clone and the package imports. Item 3 is "README says what the program does and how to run it" (session 5's slide: what it does, how to install, how to run). This README stops after the first part, so a stranger cannot get from the clone to a first result. Two more lines, `uv sync` and one real `uv run fares` example, would meet it.

questions.stem_md: Each situation shows one pillar or value of Scrum at work. Sort it by the one it shows best.

items.text_md: The board shows the real state: an item that fails the CI check stays in "In progress"
items.why_md: The real state of the work is visible to everyone, so there is something true to inspect.

items.text_md: The Sprint Backlog is open to the whole team and updated every day
items.why_md: Making the work visible is the first pillar; a hidden plan cannot be inspected.

items.text_md: At the Review the team runs the product and compares it with the Sprint Goal
items.why_md: Looking at the actual work at regular points, not at a report about it.

items.text_md: Before the Review the Scrum Master asks the team to check that every Done item meets the Definition of Done
items.why_md: Checking the work against the agreed bar before showing it is inspection.

items.text_md: After the Retrospective the group adds "README updated" to its Definition of Done
items.why_md: Changing how the team works because the inspection showed a gap.

items.text_md: The Product Owner reorders the backlog after the Review shows users want a different feature first
items.why_md: Changing course because of what was inspected.

items.text_md: A developer tells the Daily that her item will not be finished, although she knows it is bad news
items.why_md: Saying something unwelcome is the value slide 13 ties to adaptation. Without it, nothing changes.

items.text_md: The Product Owner removes her favourite item from the backlog because the evidence says it is not worth doing
items.why_md: Acting on evidence against your own idea takes courage; the other values do not cover it.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 13: pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation; the values include courage. The pillars are a sequence (make it visible, look at it, change course), and the slide's two lines tie them to the values: "Inspection without transparency inspects a fiction. Adaptation without courage produces the same Sprint, twelve times." Courage is what turns a visible problem into a changed Sprint. To remember the plain list, use the flashcard.

questions.stem_md:
The fare-calculator group's Checkpoint 1 says `uv sync && uv run fares --help` must work from a clean clone. Ana clones the repository to `~/fare-calculator` to check it, and in the same terminal types:

```console
$ pwd
/home/ana
$ uv run fares --help
error: Failed to spawn: `fares`
  cause: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

She writes to the group: "The first CP1 item fails from a clean clone. We cannot tag `v0.1`." What is the right reading?

options.text_md: She ran the command in her home folder, not in the clone; check again from inside `~/fare-calculator` before judging the item
options.why_md: `pwd` shows `/home/ana`. uv finds the project from the current folder and its parents, so outside the clone there is no `fares` to start. The check was run in the wrong place.

options.text_md: The item fails: `[project.scripts]` does not match the command, so rename the entry and tag again
options.why_md: `Failed to spawn` can mean that, but only after the check is run inside the project. From her home folder every project command fails the same way.

options.text_md: The item fails because `uv sync` was not run; running it from her home folder first would fix it
options.why_md: `uv sync` also needs a project: from `/home/ana` it prints `No `pyproject.toml` found`. We ran it.

options.text_md: The item is met: a clean clone only has to exist, and the command is checked later at the tag
options.why_md: Checkpoint 1 is three binary items "checkable before you submit", and the first is the command working from a clean clone. It is checked inside the clone.

questions.explanation_md: A Definition of Done is only useful if the check is run properly (slide 10: one you cannot check yourself is a wish). Ana's red is a false red. Read the prompt: `pwd` prints `/home/ana`, not the clone, so `uv run fares` looks for the project in the wrong place and fails with the same `Failed to spawn` message a real mismatch gives. The lab's table lists that message with causes inside the project, so the reading needs the folder as well as the error. `cd ~/fare-calculator && uv sync && uv run fares --help` is the real check. Real run: the same command in a folder without a project printed the error shown.
questions.source_ref: S4 slides 10, 17, 23; S5 slide 13; labs/01-scaffold.md troubleshooting

questions.stem_md:
The fare-calculator group (topic: zones, travelcards, the cheapest way to cover a week) disagrees about the top of its Product Backlog. Two candidates:

- **A:** "Write `zones.py` with a dictionary of fares and one function per travelcard"
- **B:** "As a commuter, I can enter the trips I make in a week and see the cheapest ticket or travelcard for them, so that I do not overpay"

parts.prompt_md: In one sentence each, what does A describe and what does B describe?
parts.model_answer_md: A describes work the team would do, and how it would build it; B describes what a commuter can do with the program, and why they want it.
rubric: Says A is a task (code to write) rather than something a user gets, and B is an outcome for a user with its benefit
parts.weak_answers_md: "A is technical and B is not" is only half the point: name A as a task (work you do) and B as an outcome (what a user gets). "B is longer" or "B uses the template" describes the form, not the difference, which is that B says who gains what.

parts.prompt_md: Which one belongs in the Product Backlog, and why? Answer from the point of view of whoever has to order the backlog.
parts.model_answer_md: B. It names a user and a benefit, so it can be ordered by value against other items, and anyone can tell when it is done by running the program. A is a task nobody can tell is finished, and it decides how (a dictionary), which is the Developers' call.
rubric: Chooses B because it is an outcome with a stated benefit that can be ordered by value
Says A is a task (nobody can tell when it is done) or prescribes how, which belongs to the Developers
parts.weak_answers_md: "B, because it follows the template" gets half at most: say what the template gives (a user, a benefit, something you can check). Choosing A "because it is more concrete" confuses precise with checkable: A is precise about code but says nothing a user gets, so nobody can order it by value or say when it is done.

parts.prompt_md: Describe in words one check that would show B is done, and the line of a Definition of Done it satisfies.
parts.model_answer_md: A test: a week with many zone-1 trips gets the travelcard, and a week with one trip gets a single ticket. It meets "there is at least one test for the new behaviour", and it runs inside the green CI check.
rubric: A concrete check in words, with an input and the expected result
Links it to a Definition of Done line: a test for the new behaviour, or the CI check being green
parts.weak_answers_md: "Test that it works" names no input and no expected result, so it checks nothing. A check on A's dictionary ("it has every zone") tests the shape of the code, not what the commuter gets. A check without the DoD line, or the line without a check, gets half.

questions.explanation_md: This is the teacher's compare shape applied to the backlog: two candidates, which is better for the person who has to use it, and one check in words. The brief defines an item as "an outcome a user gets, not a task you perform", small enough to finish in a sitting and something you can tell is done, written as `As a <kind of user>, I can <do something>, so that <benefit>`. B fits; A is a task, and it also decides how the work is done, which slide 7 gives to the Developers. The check in part 3 is what makes B done under a Definition of Done written as "things you can check, not things you can hope".
questions.source_ref: Backlog brief (moodle/project-pages.md); S4 slides 7, 9, 30; sample Q8 shape

parts.prompt_md: Is the peak-fare item done? Answer in terms of the group's Definition of Done.
parts.model_answer_md: No. CI is red, so the item misses the Definition of Done: it is not done, does not ship, and is not shown as finished tomorrow.
rubric: Says not done because CI is red and the DoD requires green, so the item does not ship
parts.weak_answers_md: "Nearly done, only the types are wrong" is "done except for...", which session 4 says is not admissible. "Done, because the tests pass" ignores that the Types step is part of the same check, and the check is the line in the DoD.

parts.prompt_md: Which error could crash the program for a real user, and how? What kind of error is the other one?
parts.model_answer_md: Line 10: a zone that is not in the table, such as 4, makes `find_fare` return `None`, and adding 0.50 to `None` raises a `TypeError`: None not handled. Line 13 is a missing annotation; it crashes nothing by itself.
rubric: Names line 10 and the input that crashes it: an unknown zone makes `find_fare` return None, and None + 0.50 fails
Classifies line 13 as a missing annotation that does not crash by itself
parts.weak_answers_md: "Line 13, because the function has no types" confuses a missing hint with a crash: Python runs it fine. Saying line 10 is wrong "because of the types" without naming the input that triggers it (a zone not in the table) misses the user's view: the crash happens at run time, for a real zone number.

parts.prompt_md: Iker proposes adding `# type: ignore` to both lines so CI is green for the Review, and fixing them next Sprint. Do you accept? Give your reasoning in session 4's terms.
parts.model_answer_md: No. CI would go green but zone 4 would still crash, so the Review would inspect a fiction and the Definition of Done would mean nothing. Fix both tonight (handle the unknown zone with a clear message, add the hint) or say at the Review that the item is not done.
rubric: Rejects it: silencing the check leaves the crash for an unknown zone in place
Uses session 4: a green check that hides a known bug makes the Review inspect a fiction (transparency), or the DoD becomes decoration
Gives the honest alternative: fix both errors, or present the item as not done
parts.weak_answers_md: "Yes, if they fix it next Sprint" ships a known crash and calls it done. "No, ignores are bad style" gives no reason anyone can act on: say what stays broken (zone 4 still crashes) and what the Review would then be looking at. Changing `find_fare` to return `float` does not help either: mypy then flags the line that can return `None`, because the missing zone is still possible.

questions.explanation_md: This is the teacher's read-tool-output shape with a Scrum ending. Line 10 is the None-not-handled kind: an unknown zone makes `find_fare` return `None`, and adding the surcharge to `None` raises `TypeError`, session 7's "crash at 2 a.m.". Line 13 is a missing annotation. Under the group's Definition of Done the item is not done while CI is red. With `# type: ignore` on both lines mypy reports no issues, yet `peak_fare(4)` still crashes: the check would be green and false. The Review would then inspect a fiction, which is what the transparency pillar exists to prevent.

questions.stem_md: At the habit-tracker group's Daily, the Product Owner joins. After the first developer speaks, she starts discussing which items should be dropped from the Sprint and asks each developer to justify their progress to her. The Daily ends after forty minutes. In session 4's terms, what went wrong?

options.text_md: Nothing: the PO orders the work, so the Daily is the natural place to re-plan it
options.why_md: The PO orders the Product Backlog, but the Daily is fifteen minutes for the Developers to check progress towards the Sprint Goal, not a planning meeting.

options.text_md: The PO should not have come: the Daily is for the Developers, and she has no place there
options.why_md: Slide 12 says the PO can join. What went wrong is what she did once she was there, not that she came.

options.text_md: The Scrum Master should have collected the reports instead, so the PO could leave early
options.why_md: The Scrum Master is not a manager either; the Daily is not a status report to anyone.

options.text_md: She may join but is not expected to take part; the Daily became a report to her
options.why_md: Slide 12: the PO can join but is not expected to participate. Turning the Daily into a report to her also broke its fifteen-minute time-box.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 12: "Daily Scrum is not a status report to a manager. Fifteen minutes, for the Developers. PO can join but not expected to participate." Here the PO turns the Daily into a report to her and a re-planning session, and it runs to forty minutes. Each developer should take about a minute: latest work, what they will work on next, any blockers. Her being there is allowed; her taking over is not. If she thinks the Sprint's scope is wrong, she can raise it with the Developers after the Daily; in the extreme, the PO retains the power to cancel the Sprint.

questions.stem_md: The task-manager group has forty well-written backlog items, ordered by the Product Owner, and a Definition of Done. At the Review a visitor asks what the product as a whole is for. Three team members give three different answers. Which commitment is missing?

options.text_md: The Product Goal: the Product Backlog's commitment, what the whole backlog is heading towards
options.why_md: Slide 8: Product Backlog → Product Goal. Without it, the backlog is "just a list" and nobody can say what the product is for.

options.text_md: The Sprint Goal: the commitment that says what the current Sprint is for
options.why_md: The Sprint Goal belongs to the Sprint Backlog and covers one Sprint. The visitor asked about the product as a whole.

options.text_md: The Definition of Done: the quality bar every Increment has to meet
options.why_md: The group has one. It says how good finished work must be, not what the product is for.

options.text_md: More backlog items: with another forty the purpose would become clear
options.why_md: More items do not answer the question. Slide 8: "Without its commitment, it is just a list."

questions.explanation_md: Slide 8 gives each artifact a commitment: Product Backlog → Product Goal, Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal, Increment → Definition of Done. Each exists to make something visible, and "without its commitment, it is just a list". The group has a good list and a quality bar, but nothing that says where the list is heading, so the team members each supply their own purpose. A Product Goal is one sentence that every backlog item can be tested against. The Sprint Goal is the smaller version for one Sprint.
